/guides/uk-arthritis.bodyHtml:
What Is Arthritis?

Arthritis is not one disease. It is an umbrella term for more than 100 conditions. They all cause pain, swelling and stiffness in or around the joints.

In the UK, about 10 million people live with arthritis (Versus Arthritis, now Arthritis UK, 2024). It is one of the most common long-term health conditions in the country. It affects people of all ages and backgrounds. It is more common in women and in people over 45.

The Main Types at a Glance

  • Osteoarthritis (OA) — the "wear and tear" type. Cartilage in the joints thins over time.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) — an autoimmune type. The immune system attacks the joint lining.
  • Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) — linked to the skin condition psoriasis.
  • Gout — caused by uric acid crystals in the joints.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — mainly affects the spine.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis — the main type in children.

How Common Is Arthritis in the UK?

Arthritis affects about 1 in 6 adults in the UK. That is roughly 10 million people. It is the top cause of pain and disability in the country.

Around 8.75 million people aged 45 and over in the UK have sought treatment for osteoarthritis (Arthritis Research UK, now Arthritis UK, 2013; cited by NICE CKS). Rheumatoid arthritis affects around 400,000 people. Psoriatic arthritis affects around 146,000.

The Cost to the UK

The numbers are huge. Arthritis and bone or joint problems make up 30% of all GP visits in England. They are the biggest cause of time off work.

The total cost to the UK is about £12.6 billion a year in lost work, sick days and care (Versus Arthritis, now Arthritis UK, 2024). Even so, arthritis gets far less research funding than cancer or heart disease.

Cases are rising. The UK is ageing. More people are living with obesity and sitting more. By 2030, over 12 million people in the UK are expected to have arthritis.

Types of Arthritis Explained

Osteoarthritis (OA)

Osteoarthritis is the most common type. Around 8.75 million people aged 45 and over in the UK have sought treatment for it (Arthritis Research UK, now Arthritis UK, 2013; cited by NICE CKS). It is often called the "wear and tear" type. The cartilage cushioning the joints breaks down over time.

As cartilage thins, bones start to rub. This causes pain, swelling and stiffness. The joints hit hardest are the knees, hips, hands, spine and feet.

Who is at risk

  • Being over 45
  • Being female
  • Carrying extra weight
  • Past joint injury
  • Repeat strain at work
  • Family history

Common symptoms

  • Morning stiffness that eases within 30 minutes
  • Pain that gets worse with activity
  • A grating or crackling feeling (crepitus)
  • Swelling around the joint
  • Slow loss of flexibility

There is no cure for OA. But symptoms can be managed well. Useful steps include weight loss, gentle exercise, physiotherapy and pain relief. In severe cases, joint replacement surgery can help.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

RA is an autoimmune disease. It affects about 400,000 people in the UK. The immune system attacks the joint lining. This causes long-term inflammation that can damage cartilage and bone.

RA often affects joints on both sides of the body. For example, both wrists or both knees. It can also affect the lungs, heart and eyes.

Symptoms to watch for

  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Pain and swelling in the hands, wrists or feet
  • Tiredness and feeling unwell

Early diagnosis matters a lot. NICE guidelines say a GP should refer you to a rheumatologist within 3 working days if RA is suspected. Early treatment with drugs like methotrexate can stop lasting joint damage.

Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)

PsA affects up to 30% of people with psoriasis. That is about 146,000 people in the UK. It causes joint pain, stiffness and swelling alongside skin patches.

PsA often hits the fingers and toes. This can cause swollen "sausage digits". It can also affect the spine and the spots where tendons join bone.

Other Types

  • Gout — affects about 1.6 million people. Caused by uric acid crystals, often in the big toe.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — mainly the spine. Can cause inflammatory back pain and stiffening over time.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) — the main type in children. Around 15,000 under-16s in the UK.
  • Reactive arthritis — starts after an infection.
  • Fibromyalgia — not arthritis, but a related chronic pain condition. Affects an estimated 2.9 million UK adults.

Symptoms and Diagnosis

Most types of arthritis share a core set of symptoms:

  • Joint pain — from a dull ache to sharp pain
  • Stiffness — often after rest or in the morning
  • Swelling — from inflammation or fluid
  • Redness and warmth — around the joint
  • Less movement — harder to bend, grip or walk
  • Fatigue — common in RA and other inflammatory types
  • Crepitus — grinding, clicking or popping

How diagnosis works

Most people start with a GP visit. The GP may ask for blood tests. These can include CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies. X-rays are common too. MRI or ultrasound may be used in some cases.

Your GP can refer you to a rheumatologist. Many practices also let you see a physiotherapist first, without a GP referral, under the First Contact Practitioner scheme.

Treatment Options in the UK

Treatment depends on the type and how severe the arthritis is. Most plans mix three things: self-care, medication and (sometimes) surgery.

Conservative Management

  • Exercise — the most effective non-drug treatment. Try walking, swimming or cycling.
  • Weight management — losing just 5% of body weight can cut knee pain in OA.
  • Physiotherapy — guided exercises, hands-on therapy and electrotherapy.
  • Occupational therapy — joint protection, aids and home changes.
  • Diet — a Mediterranean-style diet can lower inflammation.

Medications

  • Paracetamol — first choice for mild OA pain
  • NSAIDs — such as ibuprofen or naproxen
  • Steroid injections — short-term relief for badly inflamed joints
  • DMARDs — such as methotrexate for RA and PsA
  • Biologics — such as adalimumab or etanercept for severe cases
  • JAK inhibitors — newer targeted drugs for RA

Surgical Options

  • Joint replacement — knee and hip replacements are very successful. Over 160,000 are done each year in the UK.
  • Arthroscopy — keyhole surgery for diagnosis or minor repairs.
  • Joint fusion — used for badly damaged small joints.

Living Well With Arthritis

Managing arthritis is about more than medicine. The best results come from a whole-person plan. This means activity, food, mental health support and community.

Seven habits that help

  • Stay active — aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
  • Eat well — a Mediterranean-style diet rich in oily fish, fruit, veg and whole grains.
  • Manage stress — try mindfulness, meditation or CBT.
  • Sleep well — aim for 7–9 hours. Poor sleep makes pain feel worse.
  • Pace yourself — mix activity with rest to avoid flare-ups.
  • Use aids — jar openers, long-handled reachers and walking aids can help a lot.
  • Connect with others — peer groups reduce isolation and improve coping.

Mental Health and Arthritis

Chronic pain wears people down. People with arthritis are 2–3 times more likely to have depression or anxiety (Arthritis Research UK). The link works both ways. Pain lowers mood, and low mood makes pain feel worse.

Where to get help

  • UK healthcare Talking Therapies (IAPT) — free talking therapy and CBT. Self-referral is available.
  • Pain management programmes — group programmes mixing physio, psychology and OT.
  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) helpline — 0800 5200 520 (free, weekdays).
  • Mind — 0300 123 3393 for general mental health support.

Arthritis in Younger People

Many people think arthritis only affects older adults. That is a myth.

About 15,000 children in the UK have juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Many adults in their 20s and 30s also develop types like RA, PsA or ankylosing spondylitis.

Young people with arthritis face extra challenges. These can include study, work, relationships and family planning. Charities like Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and NRAS offer tailored support.

Research and Future Treatments

UK arthritis research is moving fast. Key areas include:

  • Regenerative medicine — stem cell therapy to regrow cartilage
  • Precision medicine — using DNA to pick the best drug for each person
  • Digital health — apps, wearables and remote monitoring
  • New biologics — drugs that target inflammation more precisely
  • The gut microbiome — how gut bacteria affect autoimmune arthritis

Main UK funders include Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) (over £9 million a year), the NIHR and the Medical Research Council. Clinical trials are open via the NIHR Clinical Research Network.

Key UK Resources

  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) — arthritis-uk.org — helpline: 0800 5200 520
  • NRAS — nras.org.uk — helpline: 0800 298 7650
  • Health and social care (UK Government) — NHS services
  • Arthritis Action — arthritisaction.org.uk
  • Citizens Advice — help with benefits and PIP
  • Living With Arthritis — free virtual physio, diet plans and community support

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide draws on public data from the UK health service, NICE guidelines (NG100, NG226, CG79), Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and NRAS. It also uses peer-reviewed research from The Lancet, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases and the BMJ. Figures are the most recent available as of 2024.

This page is for information only. It is not medical advice. Always speak to your GP or rheumatologist about your own care.

faqs.q: How many people in the UK have arthritis?
faqs.a: Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis — roughly 1 in 6 adults. Osteoarthritis is by far the most common type: around 8.75 million people aged 45 and over in the UK have sought treatment for it (Arthritis Research UK, now Arthritis UK, 2013; cited by NICE CKS). It is followed by rheumatoid arthritis (around 400,000) and psoriatic arthritis (around 146,000).

faqs.q: What is the most common type of arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: Osteoarthritis is the most common type, accounting for the large majority of cases. It is sometimes called 'wear and tear' arthritis and most often affects the knees, hips, hands and spine.

faqs.q: Is arthritis a disability in the UK?
faqs.a: Arthritis is recognised as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 when it has a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities. Many people with arthritis qualify for reasonable workplace adjustments and may be eligible for Personal Independence Payment (PIP).

faqs.q: Can arthritis be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure for most forms of arthritis, but symptoms can be managed effectively with a combination of exercise, weight management, anti-inflammatory diet, physiotherapy and — for inflammatory types — disease-modifying medications that can put the condition into remission.

faqs.q: What is the best treatment for arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: NICE guidelines (NG226) recommend a core package of exercise, weight management and patient education first, with medications, physiotherapy and joint replacement surgery added as needed. For inflammatory arthritis, early DMARD treatment from a rheumatology team is critical.

faqs.q: How long do I have to wait to see a rheumatologist on the public health service?
faqs.a: Waiting times vary widely. The national target is 18 weeks from referral to first appointment, but actual waits range from around 8 weeks in some areas to over 30 weeks in others. Urgent inflammatory arthritis referrals are typically seen within 3 weeks.

/guides/health-services.bodyHtml:
Overview of Arthritis Services

The National Health Service provides a comprehensive framework of arthritis care across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. From initial GP consultations through to specialist rheumatology clinics, joint replacement surgery and community rehabilitation, the public health service offers a multi-layered system of support. Understanding how to navigate this system effectively can dramatically improve your experience and outcomes.

In England alone, musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions account for approximately 30% of all GP consultations (public health data, 2023). The health service spends an estimated £10.2 billion annually on musculoskeletal care, making it one of the largest areas of healthcare expenditure. Despite this, waiting times for rheumatology appointments have increased significantly since 2020, with some areas reporting waits of 6–12 months for a first specialist appointment.

Your GP and First Contact Physiotherapists

Your journey through the arthritis care pathway typically begins with your General Practitioner (GP). GPs are trained to assess joint pain, order initial blood tests and imaging, prescribe first-line medications, and refer to specialists when necessary.

However, one of the most significant recent developments in the public health service musculoskeletal care is the introduction of First Contact Practitioners (FCPs). These are specialist physiotherapists embedded within GP practices who can assess, diagnose and manage musculoskeletal conditions — including arthritis — without requiring a GP referral. Since 2019, the public health service has trained and deployed over 4,000 FCPs across England as part of the Additional Roles Reimbursement Scheme (ARRS).

FCPs can:

  • Assess your joint symptoms on the same day or within days
  • Order X-rays and blood tests
  • Provide exercise programmes and self-management advice
  • Refer directly to rheumatology, orthopaedics or other specialists
  • Prescribe certain medications (if qualified as an independent prescriber)

To access an FCP, simply contact your GP practice and ask to book an appointment with the musculoskeletal physiotherapist or first contact practitioner. Not all practices have one, but the number is growing rapidly.

Getting a Rheumatology Referral

If your GP or FCP suspects an inflammatory type of arthritis (such as RA, PsA or ankylosing spondylitis), they should refer you to a rheumatologist — a hospital-based consultant who specialises in inflammatory joint diseases. NICE guidelines (NG100) state that suspected RA should be referred urgently, ideally within 3 working days, because early treatment with DMARDs within the first 12 weeks of symptom onset significantly improves long-term outcomes.

What to expect at your first rheumatology appointment:

  • A thorough clinical examination of your joints
  • Review of blood tests (CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP antibodies)
  • Possible ultrasound scan of affected joints (increasingly done in clinic)
  • Discussion of treatment options, typically starting with methotrexate for RA
  • Goal-setting using a treat-to-target approach (aiming for low disease activity or remission)

The national standard for rheumatology is an 18-week referral-to-treatment (RTT) target. However, actual waiting times vary considerably by region. As of 2024, the average wait for a rheumatology first appointment in England is approximately 14 weeks, but some Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) report waits exceeding 26 weeks.

Tips for faster access:

  • Ask your GP to mark the referral as urgent if inflammatory arthritis is suspected
  • Request a choose and book appointment — you may find shorter waits at a hospital further away
  • Some local health trusts offer triage services where a rheumatology nurse reviews referrals and fast-tracks urgent cases
  • Check if your area has an Early Inflammatory Arthritis (EIA) clinic — these are dedicated rapid-access services

Public Health Physiotherapy for Arthritis

Physiotherapy is a cornerstone of arthritis management and is available free through the public health service. NICE guidelines recommend exercise therapy as a first-line treatment for osteoarthritis, ahead of medication. public health physiotherapy services include:

  • Individual assessment — a physiotherapist evaluates your mobility, strength, pain and function
  • Tailored exercise programmes — specific to your joints and condition
  • Group exercise classes — many local health trusts run arthritis-specific group sessions
  • Hydrotherapy — warm-water exercise sessions available at some hospitals
  • Manual therapy — hands-on treatment for joint mobilisation
  • Education and self-management — teaching you to manage symptoms independently

Access is via GP or FCP referral, or in some areas through self-referral. The health service website (NHS services) lists self-referral physiotherapy services near you. Waiting times for public health physiotherapy typically range from 4–12 weeks.

Public Pain Management Programmes

For people with chronic arthritis pain that hasn't responded adequately to standard treatments, the public health service offers multidisciplinary pain management programmes (PMPs). These are typically run by a team including a pain consultant, psychologist, physiotherapist and occupational therapist.

PMPs focus on:

  • Understanding pain — pain neuroscience education
  • Pacing and activity management — avoiding boom-bust cycles
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) — changing unhelpful pain-related thoughts and behaviours
  • Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) — psychological flexibility
  • Graded exercise — building activity levels safely
  • Medication review — optimising or reducing pain medication

Referral is typically through your GP or rheumatologist. PMPs are available in most the public health service regions, though waiting times can be 6–18 months.

Joint Replacement Surgery through the public health service

When conservative treatments fail to adequately manage pain and function, joint replacement surgery may be recommended. The health service performs over 160,000 hip and knee replacements annually, making them among the most common and successful operations in the public health service (NJR, 2024).

Key facts about the public health service joint replacement:

  • Success rates — over 95% of patients report significant pain reduction; 90% of knee replacements last 15+ years
  • Eligibility — based on clinical need, not age; assessed by orthopaedic surgeon
  • Waiting times — the public health service target is 18 weeks, but actual waits average 6–12 months in 2024
  • Prehabilitation — many trusts now offer "prehab" programmes to optimise fitness before surgery
  • Recovery — most patients return to normal activities within 3–6 months
  • Cost — fully funded through the public health service; no charge to the patient

The National Joint Registry (NJR) tracks every joint replacement performed in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man, ensuring quality and safety monitoring.

Medications Available through the public health service

The health service provides all medically necessary arthritis medications at standard prescription cost (currently £9.90 per item in England as of 2024; free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). Key medications include:

  • Paracetamol and NSAIDs — first-line pain relief
  • Corticosteroids — short courses for flares, injections for localised inflammation
  • DMARDs — methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide
  • Biologics — adalimumab (Humira), etanercept (Enbrel), rituximab, tocilizumab, secukinumab
  • JAK inhibitors — tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib

If you take regular prescribed medication, a Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC) can save significant money. A 12-month PPC costs £111.60 (2024) and covers unlimited prescriptions — worthwhile if you have more than 11 items per year.

Mental Health Support Through the Public Health System

The health service recognises the profound impact of chronic pain on mental health. Services available include:

  • IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies) — free CBT and counselling, self-referral available at NHS services
  • Public health pain psychology — specialist psychologists within pain management teams
  • Social prescribing — link workers who connect you with community activities, support groups and local services
  • Crisis support — 111 helpline (option 2 for mental health crisis) or Samaritans 116 123

Differences Across the UK Nations

Healthcare is devolved in the UK, meaning services differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland:

  • Scotland — Scotland's health service provides free prescriptions for all. Musculoskeletal services are managed through Health Boards. The Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) publishes its own clinical guidelines.
  • Wales — Wales's health service also provides free prescriptions. Arthritis care is delivered through Local Health Boards. Wales has invested in community musculoskeletal services.
  • Northern Ireland — Free prescriptions. Services delivered through Health and Social Care (HSC) trusts. Waiting times have historically been longer than England.
  • England — Standard prescription charges apply (unless exempt). Services commissioned by Integrated Care Boards (ICBs). Most FCPs are deployed here.

How to Get the Most From Arthritis Services

  • Prepare for appointments — write down your symptoms, questions and medication list
  • Ask about self-referral — for physiotherapy, IAPT and some community services
  • Use the public health service online services — book appointments, order repeat prescriptions and view records through the public health service App
  • Request a care plan — if you have a long-term condition, you're entitled to an annual review and personalised care plan
  • Know your rights — the public health service Constitution gives you the right to treatment within 18 weeks of referral
  • Consider Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) — if you're unhappy with your care
  • Join a support group — many local health trusts partner with Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) to run hospital-based support groups

Sources & Disclaimer

Information sourced from the public health service Digital, NICE guidelines (NG100, NG226, CG177, CG79), the National Joint Registry Annual Report 2024, England's health service workforce data, and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). This guide is for educational purposes and does not constitute medical advice. Always consult your healthcare team for personalised guidance.

faqs.q: How do I get a rheumatology referral in the UK?
faqs.a: Book a GP appointment and describe your joint symptoms, including pattern, duration and morning stiffness. The GP can refer you to rheumatology. Suspected inflammatory arthritis (e.g. swollen small joints with morning stiffness over 30 minutes) should trigger an urgent referral to be seen within 3 weeks.

faqs.q: What is a First Contact Physiotherapist?
faqs.a: First Contact Physiotherapists (FCPs) are senior physios working in GP practices. You can book directly without seeing a GP first. They assess musculoskeletal problems including arthritis, request scans, recommend exercises and refer on to specialists if needed.

faqs.q: How long does a hip or knee replacement waiting list take in the UK?
faqs.a: After being added to a surgical waiting list, the national target is 18 weeks from referral to treatment, but typical waits range from 6 to 18+ months depending on region. Use our waiting-time calculator for a regional estimate.

faqs.q: Is physiotherapy free for arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: Yes — physiotherapy is free on the public health service when referred by a GP, First Contact Physio or hospital clinician. Many areas also offer self-referral. Waits vary; private physiotherapy typically costs £40–£70 per session if you want faster access.

faqs.q: Can I get a joint injection for arthritis on the public health service?
faqs.a: Yes. Steroid (cortisone) injections for inflamed joints, and sometimes hyaluronic-acid injections for knees, are available via GP, physio or rheumatology referral. They can provide weeks to months of pain relief but are usually limited to a few per year per joint.

faqs.q: What support is available for mental health alongside arthritis?
faqs.a: Chronic pain and arthritis are linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety. The public health service offers Talking Therapies (self-referral in England), pain-management programmes that include psychological support, and dedicated chronic-pain services. Mention low mood to your GP — it's recognised as part of arthritis care.

/guides/diet.bodyHtml:
Why Diet Matters for Arthritis

The relationship between diet and arthritis is one of the most researched areas in rheumatology. While no single food can cure arthritis, mounting evidence demonstrates that what you eat can significantly influence inflammation levels, pain intensity, joint stiffness, disease activity and even the effectiveness of medications. Reviews of Mediterranean-style and anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (including work summarised for clinicians in journals such as Nutrients) suggest diet can support lower pain and inflammatory markers for some people — effects vary, and diet does not replace prescribed treatment.

For people with osteoarthritis, diet also plays a critical role in weight management. Excess weight is the single most modifiable risk factor for OA: every 1 kg of body weight lost reduces the load on each knee by approximately 4 kg with every step (Messier et al., 2013). For overweight individuals with knee OA, losing just 5–10% of body weight can produce clinically meaningful reductions in pain and improvements in function.

The Mediterranean Diet: The Gold Standard

The Mediterranean diet is the most extensively studied dietary pattern for arthritis and chronic inflammation. It consistently outperforms other diets in clinical trials for reducing inflammatory markers, joint pain and cardiovascular risk — which is elevated in people with inflammatory arthritis.

Want a plan to follow this week? See the focused 7-day Mediterranean eating plan for arthritis — UK shopping list, recipes and what to eat freely, weekly and rarely.

Core Principles

  • Abundant vegetables and fruits — aim for 7+ portions daily, focusing on colourful varieties rich in antioxidants (berries, leafy greens, tomatoes, peppers, beetroot)
  • Wholegrains — oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread, quinoa, bulgur wheat
  • Healthy fats — extra virgin olive oil as the primary fat source (rich in oleocanthal, which has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory properties)
  • Oily fish — at least 2 portions per week (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout) for omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA
  • Legumes and pulses — lentils, chickpeas, beans — excellent protein and fibre sources
  • Nuts and seeds — walnuts (highest plant omega-3), almonds, flaxseeds, chia seeds
  • Herbs and spices — turmeric, ginger, garlic, oregano, rosemary — many have documented anti-inflammatory properties
  • Moderate dairy — yoghurt and cheese in moderation; fermented dairy supports gut health
  • Limited red meat — no more than 1–2 portions per week; processed meats avoided
  • Limited sugar and refined carbohydrates — these promote inflammation

A landmark 2023 trial in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases found that RA patients following a Mediterranean diet for 16 weeks experienced a significant reduction in DAS28 scores (a composite measure of disease activity) compared to controls, with improvements in fatigue and quality of life.

Key Anti-Inflammatory Foods

Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Omega-3s are the most well-evidenced dietary component for arthritis. EPA and DHA — found primarily in oily fish — are converted into anti-inflammatory compounds called resolvins and protectins that actively help resolve inflammation. A 2017 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology found that fish oil supplementation (2–4 g/day of combined EPA/DHA) significantly reduced joint pain, morning stiffness and NSAID use in RA patients.

Best food sources:

  • Salmon (wild-caught) — 2.2 g omega-3 per 100 g
  • Mackerel — 2.6 g per 100 g
  • Sardines — 1.5 g per 100 g
  • Trout — 1.0 g per 100 g
  • Walnuts — 2.5 g ALA (plant omega-3) per 30 g
  • Flaxseeds — 6.7 g ALA per 30 g (ground for absorption)
  • Chia seeds — 5.0 g ALA per 30 g

Recommendation: Aim for 2 portions of oily fish per week plus daily plant sources. If you don't eat fish, consider an algae-based omega-3 supplement (providing EPA/DHA directly).

Turmeric and Curcumin

Turmeric's active compound, curcumin, is one of the most extensively studied natural anti-inflammatory agents. It works by blocking NF-ÎºB — a master regulator of inflammation — and inhibiting COX-2 and LOX enzymes (similar mechanisms to NSAIDs like ibuprofen). A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Medicinal Food concluded that 1,000 mg/day of curcumin significantly reduced pain and improved function in knee OA patients.

Key considerations:

  • Curcumin has poor bioavailability on its own — pairing with black pepper (piperine) increases absorption by up to 2,000%
  • Study curcumin products differ from cooking turmeric — ask a clinician or pharmacist before using concentrated supplements
  • Some trials show curcumin provides comparable pain relief to diclofenac with fewer side effects
  • Consult your doctor if taking blood thinners or diabetes medication, as curcumin may interact

Ginger

Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols — bioactive compounds with anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. A 2015 meta-analysis of 5 randomised controlled trials found that ginger supplementation (500–1,000 mg/day) significantly reduced OA pain compared to placebo. Fresh ginger can be used in cooking (1–2 cm fresh root daily) or as a tea.

Berries and Antioxidant-Rich Foods

Berries — particularly blueberries, strawberries, cherries and blackcurrants — are rich in anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress and inflammation. Tart cherry juice has been specifically studied for gout, where it has been shown to reduce uric acid levels and flare frequency. Other antioxidant-rich foods include dark leafy greens (kale, spinach), beetroot, sweet potatoes and dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa).

Foods That May Worsen Arthritis

While individual responses vary, certain foods are consistently associated with increased inflammation and worsened arthritis symptoms:

  • Processed and ultra-processed foods — ready meals, crisps, biscuits, processed meats (bacon, sausages, ham) — high in advanced glycation end products (AGEs) that promote inflammation
  • Added sugars — fizzy drinks, sweets, cakes — trigger inflammatory cytokine release
  • Refined carbohydrates — white bread, white pasta, pastries — spike blood sugar and insulin, promoting inflammation
  • Excessive alcohol — increases uric acid (worsens gout) and systemic inflammation
  • Excessive omega-6 fatty acids — found in sunflower oil, corn oil and many processed foods — when consumed in excess relative to omega-3, these promote pro-inflammatory pathways
  • Trans fats — hydrogenated oils found in some margarines and commercial baked goods
  • Excessive red meat — particularly processed meats, which contain nitrites and saturated fats

Supplements: What the Evidence Says

Glucosamine and Chondroitin

These are the most widely used OA supplements in the UK. Evidence is mixed: a 2018 Cochrane review found glucosamine provides small, uncertain benefits for pain compared to placebo. Chondroitin alone showed similarly modest effects. Combined glucosamine/chondroitin may offer slightly better outcomes, but the evidence is not strong enough for NICE to recommend routine use.

Collagen (Hydrolysed)

Emerging research suggests hydrolysed collagen peptides (10 g/day) may modestly reduce joint pain and stiffness in OA. A 2019 meta-analysis in International Orthopaedics found statistically significant improvements in pain and function, though effect sizes were small. Collagen is generally well-tolerated.

Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common in the UK (affecting up to 1 in 5 adults) and is associated with worse arthritis outcomes. The health service recommends all UK adults take a 10 mcg (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. People with inflammatory arthritis may benefit from higher doses (discuss with your doctor).

Fish Oil (Omega-3 Supplements)

If you don't consume enough oily fish, a high-quality fish oil supplement providing 1–3 g of combined EPA/DHA daily is the most well-evidenced supplement for arthritis. Look for purified, sustainably sourced products with high EPA content. Algae-based alternatives are equally effective for vegetarians and vegans.

Sample 7-Day Anti-Inflammatory Meal Plan

This plan follows Mediterranean diet principles and provides approximately 1,800–2,000 kcal/day:

Day 1

  • Breakfast: Overnight oats with blueberries, walnuts, chia seeds and honey
  • Lunch: Mediterranean salad with chickpeas, roasted peppers, feta, olives, extra virgin olive oil dressing
  • Dinner: Baked salmon with sweet potato, broccoli and turmeric-ginger sauce
  • Snack: Apple slices with almond butter

Day 2

  • Breakfast: Spinach and mushroom omelette with wholemeal toast
  • Lunch: Lentil and vegetable soup with crusty wholegrain bread
  • Dinner: Grilled mackerel with quinoa tabbouleh and roasted courgettes
  • Snack: Handful of mixed nuts and dried cranberries

Day 3

  • Breakfast: Greek yoghurt with strawberries, ground flaxseed and granola
  • Lunch: Avocado and smoked salmon on rye bread with cherry tomatoes
  • Dinner: Chicken and vegetable stir-fry with ginger, garlic and brown rice
  • Snack: Hummus with carrot and cucumber sticks

Day 4–7

Continue rotating fish (2–3 times), lean poultry, legume-based meals and plenty of colourful vegetables. Include turmeric, ginger and garlic regularly. Use extra virgin olive oil for cooking and dressings. Stay hydrated with water, green tea and ginger tea.

Gut Health and Arthritis

Emerging research links the gut microbiome to inflammatory arthritis. An imbalanced gut microbiome (dysbiosis) may trigger or worsen autoimmune responses in conditions like RA and PsA. To support gut health:

  • Eat 30+ different plant foods per week — diversity feeds diverse beneficial bacteria
  • Include fermented foods — kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, live yoghurt, miso
  • Consume prebiotic fibre — garlic, onions, leeks, asparagus, bananas, oats
  • Limit artificial sweeteners and emulsifiers — these may disrupt gut bacteria

Weight Management for Joint Health

Maintaining a healthy weight is arguably the most impactful dietary intervention for OA. Evidence-based strategies include:

  • Focus on nutrient-dense, high-satiety foods — vegetables, protein, wholegrains and healthy fats keep you fuller for longer
  • Avoid crash diets — they lead to muscle loss, which worsens joint instability
  • Aim for gradual weight loss — 0.5–1 kg per week is sustainable and preserves muscle mass
  • Combine dietary changes with regular low-impact exercise — walking, swimming, cycling
  • Consider portion control rather than food restriction — using smaller plates and mindful eating techniques

The NICE guidelines for OA (NG226) specifically recommend weight loss as a first-line treatment alongside exercise, stating it should be offered before medication.

Practical Tips for UK Shoppers

  • Budget-friendly options — tinned fish (sardines, mackerel), frozen berries, dried lentils and tinned chickpeas are just as nutritious as fresh alternatives
  • Read labels — look for traffic-light labels; aim for green on fat, sugar and salt
  • Buy seasonal UK produce — cheaper and more nutritious; farmer's markets often have better value
  • Batch cooking — prepare soups, stews and curries in bulk and freeze portions
  • Joint-friendly cooking — use electric can openers, lightweight pans and adaptive kitchen utensils from organisations like the Arthritis Action or OT referral

Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie Recipe

Beet & Berry Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie (serves 1):

  • 1 small cooked beetroot (peeled, chopped)
  • 1 cup frozen mixed berries
  • 1 banana
  • 1-inch fresh ginger (grated)
  • 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
  • 1 cup unsweetened almond milk or oat milk
  • Optional: 1 tsp turmeric powder + pinch black pepper

Blend until smooth. This provides omega-3 (flaxseed), betalains (beetroot), anthocyanins (berries), gingerols (ginger) and curcumin (turmeric) — a powerhouse of anti-inflammatory compounds in one glass.

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide is based on evidence from NICE guidelines (NG226), systematic reviews published in Nutrients, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases, British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, Journal of Medicinal Food, and guidance from the British Dietetic Association. Statistics cited are from the most recent publications available as of 2024. This information is for educational purposes only. Always consult a registered dietitian or your GP before making significant dietary changes, especially if you take medication.

faqs.q: What is an anti-inflammatory diet for arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: An anti-inflammatory diet for arthritis is essentially a Mediterranean-style pattern: plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, extra virgin olive oil, oily fish, nuts, pulses and herbs, with less ultra-processed food, sugary drinks and excess red or processed meat. NHS and UK charity guidance support this pattern for general health; it may help some people with joint symptoms but does not replace prescribed treatment.

faqs.q: What is the best arthritis diet advice in the UK?
faqs.a: The strongest evidence points to a Mediterranean / anti-inflammatory pattern plus, for knee osteoarthritis, gradual weight loss where appropriate (often discussed as around 5–10% of body weight with a clinician). Focus on oily fish twice weekly, olive oil, colourful plants and limiting ultra-processed foods — not miracle single foods.

faqs.q: What is the best diet for arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: The Mediterranean diet has the strongest evidence base for arthritis. It is rich in vegetables, fruits, wholegrains, olive oil, oily fish, nuts and pulses, and limits red meat, sugar and processed food. NHS and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) guidance supports Mediterranean-style eating for general health; individual results vary.

faqs.q: What foods make arthritis worse?
faqs.a: Ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks, refined carbohydrates, processed meats, excessive red meat and high-omega-6 vegetable oils are linked to higher inflammation. For gout specifically, alcohol (especially beer) and high-purine foods like organ meats and shellfish can trigger flares.

faqs.q: Does turmeric really help arthritis?
faqs.a: Some clinical trials of standardised curcumin extracts suggest modest pain benefit for knee osteoarthritis for some people. Cooking turmeric is healthy, but study products differ from kitchen spice. Supplements can interact with medicines (including blood-thinners) — ask a pharmacist or your clinician before starting any high-dose curcumin product.

faqs.q: How much oily fish should I eat with arthritis?
faqs.a: At least 2 portions per week, with one being oily (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout). If you don't eat fish, a daily algae-based or fish-oil supplement providing 2–4 g of combined EPA and DHA is the closest equivalent.

faqs.q: Can losing weight reduce arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Yes — for knee osteoarthritis, losing 5–10% of body weight produces clinically meaningful pain and function gains. Every 1 kg lost reduces knee load by about 4 kg with each step. Combined with exercise, weight loss is the most effective non-drug treatment for knee OA.

faqs.q: Are supplements like glucosamine and collagen worth taking?
faqs.a: Evidence is mixed and product quality varies. Some trials of glucosamine sulphate or hydrolysed collagen report modest joint comfort benefits; neither replaces diet, exercise, weight management or prescribed treatment. Discuss with a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

/guides/exercise.bodyHtml:
Why Exercise Is the Best Medicine for Arthritis

If arthritis exercise could be packaged into a pill, it would be hailed as a miracle drug. The evidence is overwhelming: regular, appropriate physical activity is the single most effective non-pharmacological treatment for arthritis. NICE guidelines (NG226) place exercise ahead of medication in the treatment hierarchy for osteoarthritis, and the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy describes it as "the most important thing you can do" for joint health.

Despite this, research shows that over 60% of adults with arthritis in the UK are insufficiently active (Sport England, 2023). Fear of worsening symptoms, lack of guidance and misinformation ("rest is best") are the primary barriers. In reality, not exercising is far more harmful: inactivity leads to muscle weakening, joint stiffness, weight gain, cardiovascular decline and worsened pain — creating a vicious cycle of deconditioning.

Benefits of regular exercise for arthritis include:

  • Pain reduction — exercise releases endorphins (natural painkillers) and reduces inflammatory markers
  • Improved joint mobility — regular movement prevents stiffness and maintains range of motion
  • Stronger muscles — muscles act as shock absorbers, protecting and stabilising joints
  • Weight management — every 1 kg lost reduces knee load by 4 kg per step
  • Better sleep — physical activity improves sleep quality, which in turn reduces pain perception
  • Improved mental health — exercise reduces depression and anxiety by up to 30% (WHO, 2022)
  • Cardiovascular protection — vital for people with inflammatory arthritis who have increased heart disease risk
  • Reduced fatigue — counterintuitively, regular exercise reduces the chronic fatigue associated with RA

Joint exercise index (start here)

Jump to the free joint-specific home routines:

  • Free knee exercises for osteoarthritis UK — 8-move NICE-aligned routine
  • Hip exercises for osteoarthritis — 8-move physio-aligned routine
  • Exercise hub — interactive library by joint
  • Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse? — safety evidence
  • Free arthritis resources UK — guides, home physio and tools (charity 1218461)

Types of Exercise for Arthritis

A balanced arthritis exercise programme should include three types of activity:

1. Aerobic (Cardiovascular) Exercise

Low-impact aerobic exercise improves cardiovascular fitness, helps manage weight, reduces inflammation and boosts mood. The health service recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week (or 75 minutes of vigorous activity). For people with arthritis, suitable options include:

  • Walking — the most accessible exercise; start with 10–15 minutes and gradually increase. Nordic walking (with poles) may improve comfort and confidence for some people, but evidence on its effect on knee loading is mixed.
  • Swimming and water aerobics — buoyancy reduces joint load by up to 90%, making it ideal for painful joints. Many the public health service and local authority pools offer arthritis-specific sessions
  • Cycling — stationary or outdoor; very low joint impact. Excellent for knee OA
  • Elliptical trainer — smooth, controlled movement without impact
  • Rowing — full-body workout with minimal joint jarring

Tip: Start at a level you can manage and build up gradually. The "talk test" is useful — if you can hold a conversation while exercising, the intensity is appropriate. If joints are sore for more than 2 hours after exercise, you may have done too much.

2. Strength (Resistance) Training

Strengthening the muscles around affected joints is critical. Strong muscles absorb shock, reduce load on joints and improve stability. A 2021 Cochrane review found that resistance training significantly reduces pain and improves function in knee OA, with effects comparable to or better than most medications.

Key exercises by joint:

Knee exercises

Full free programme: Free knee exercises for osteoarthritis UK.

  • Straight-leg raises — lie on your back, keep one leg bent and slowly raise the other, hold 5 seconds. 3 sets of 10.
  • Wall squats — lean against a wall and slide down to a comfortable squat (30–45°), hold 10 seconds. 3 sets of 5–10.
  • Step-ups — using a low step (15–20 cm), step up and down slowly. 2 sets of 10 per leg.
  • Terminal knee extensions — seated, slowly straighten your knee against resistance (using a resistance band or ankle weight). 3 sets of 10.

Hip exercises

Full free programme: Hip exercises for osteoarthritis.

  • Bridges — lie on your back with knees bent, lift hips toward the ceiling, hold 5 seconds. 3 sets of 10.
  • Clamshells — lie on your side with knees bent, keep feet together and open the top knee like a clamshell. 3 sets of 15.
  • Side-lying leg raises — lie on your side, raise the top leg slowly, hold 3 seconds. 3 sets of 10.
  • Seated hip flexion — seated, lift one knee toward your chest, hold 5 seconds. 2 sets of 10.

Hand and wrist exercises

  • Finger spreads — spread fingers wide, hold 5 seconds, relax. 10 repetitions.
  • Fist making — slowly make a fist, hold 5 seconds, release and spread. 10 repetitions.
  • Thumb touches — touch each fingertip to thumb in turn. 5 cycles per hand.
  • Wrist circles — slow circles in both directions. 10 each way.
  • Putty squeezing — therapeutic putty or stress ball. 2 minutes per hand.

Shoulder exercises

  • Pendulum swings — lean forward, let arm hang and gently swing in small circles. 1 minute each direction.
  • Wall walks — face a wall and "walk" your fingers up the wall as high as comfortable. 10 repetitions.
  • External rotation with band — elbow at side, rotate forearm outward against resistance. 3 sets of 10.

3. Flexibility and Range of Motion

Gentle stretching maintains joint flexibility, reduces stiffness and improves comfort. Best practices include:

  • Stretch daily, ideally when joints are warm (after a bath/shower or light activity)
  • Hold each stretch for 15–30 seconds; never bounce
  • Breathe normally and relax into the stretch; stop if you feel sharp pain
  • Yoga and tai chi are excellent structured flexibility programmes — both have strong evidence for arthritis benefit. Tai chi in particular has been shown to reduce pain, improve balance and reduce fall risk in older adults with OA (a 2019 BMJ meta-analysis found tai chi as effective as standard physiotherapy for knee OA)

Chair-Based Exercises

For people with significant mobility limitations or during flare-ups, chair-based exercises provide an excellent way to stay active:

  • Seated marching — lift alternate knees for 1–2 minutes
  • Seated leg extensions — straighten one knee, hold 5 seconds, lower. 10 per leg
  • Seated arm raises — lift arms to shoulder height and lower. 10 repetitions
  • Ankle circles — lift one foot and circle the ankle. 10 each direction
  • Seated trunk rotations — hands on thighs, gently rotate upper body left and right. 10 each side

These exercises are also ideal for office workers who need to combat prolonged sitting, which worsens joint stiffness.

Water-Based Exercise (Hydrotherapy)

Exercising in warm water (typically 33–36°C) is one of the most effective environments for arthritis exercise. Benefits include:

  • Buoyancy — water supports up to 90% of body weight, dramatically reducing joint load
  • Warmth — warm water relaxes muscles and increases blood flow to joints
  • Resistance — water provides natural resistance for strengthening without weights
  • Pain relief — hydrostatic pressure reduces swelling

The health service provides hydrotherapy at some hospitals (referral via GP or physiotherapist). Many local authority pools and leisure centres also offer warm-water sessions. Organisations like Swim England and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) maintain directories of arthritis-friendly swimming sessions.

Exercising During Flare-Ups

A common question is whether to exercise during a flare-up. The answer is: yes, but modify. During active flares:

  • Reduce intensity and duration — do gentle range-of-motion exercises rather than strengthening or aerobic work
  • Focus on affected joints — gentle stretching and movement to prevent stiffness
  • Use ice after exercise — 10–15 minutes to reduce inflammation
  • Listen to your body — pain during exercise that worsens or persists for more than 2 hours suggests you've overdone it
  • Avoid complete rest — prolonged inactivity during flares leads to muscle wasting and longer recovery times

Getting Started: A Progressive Programme

Weeks 1–2: Foundation

  • 5–10 minutes of gentle walking or chair exercises, 3 times per week
  • Basic stretches for affected joints (5 minutes daily)
  • Focus on establishing the habit, not intensity

Weeks 3–4: Building

  • 15–20 minutes of walking or swimming, 4 times per week
  • Add 2 strengthening exercises per affected joint area
  • Continue daily stretches

Weeks 5–8: Progressing

  • 20–30 minutes of aerobic activity, 5 times per week
  • Full strengthening routine (3 sets, 10 reps), 2–3 times per week
  • Consider joining a group class (tai chi, yoga, aqua aerobics)

Weeks 9+: Maintenance

  • 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week
  • Strength training 2–3 times per week
  • Daily flexibility work
  • Variety — mix activities to prevent boredom and overuse

Safety Guidelines

  • Warm up for 5 minutes before strengthening or vigorous activity
  • Cool down with gentle stretches afterwards
  • Use the 2-hour pain rule — if joint pain is worse 2 hours after exercise, reduce intensity next time
  • Avoid high-impact activities during flares — running, jumping, contact sports
  • Wear supportive footwear — proper shoes reduce knee and hip strain
  • Stay hydrated — dehydration can worsen joint stiffness
  • Consult a physiotherapist — for a personalised programme, especially if you're newly diagnosed or post-surgery

UK Exercise Resources

  • Living With Arthritis — free exercise programmes for every major joint
  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) — exercise guides and video library at arthritis-uk.org
  • UK Health Fitness Studio — free exercise videos at NHS services
  • Chartered Society of Physiotherapy — find a physiotherapist at csp.org.uk
  • We Are Undefeatable — campaign supporting people with long-term conditions to be active

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide is based on NICE guidelines (NG226), Cochrane systematic reviews of exercise interventions for OA and RA, the public health service physical activity guidelines, Sport England Active Lives survey data, and guidance from the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy and British Society for Rheumatology. Statistics cited are from the most recent publications available as of 2024. This information is for educational purposes only. Consult a physiotherapist or GP before starting a new exercise programme, particularly if you have severe or unstable joint disease.

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for arthritis?
faqs.a: Low-impact aerobic activity (walking, swimming, cycling), strength training and a flexibility practice such as tai chi or yoga. UK NICE guidelines (NG226) put exercise ahead of medication for osteoarthritis. The single best exercise is the one you'll actually do 3–5 times per week.

faqs.q: Should I exercise if my joints hurt?
faqs.a: Yes — moderate joint pain (up to about 4/10) during arthritis exercise is normal and safe, provided the pain settles within 24 hours. Stop and reduce intensity if pain stays high overnight, joints swell, or you experience sharp catching pain.

faqs.q: How much exercise should someone with arthritis do per week?
faqs.a: Aim for 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week (e.g. five 30-minute walks), plus 2 sessions of muscle-strengthening work, in line with UK Chief Medical Officer guidelines. Break it into 10-minute blocks if needed — short, frequent sessions count.

faqs.q: Is walking good for arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. Walking is one of the most strongly evidenced exercises for knee and hip osteoarthritis. Start with 10–15 minutes on flat ground and build up. Supportive footwear and walking poles may improve comfort and confidence for some people.

faqs.q: Is swimming better than the gym for arthritis?
faqs.a: Swimming and water-based exercise remove weight-bearing stress, making them excellent during flares or for severe joint disease. Gym-based strength training, however, is essential for protecting joints long-term — most people benefit from a combination.

faqs.q: Can I do strength training with rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes — and you should. Progressive resistance training is safe and beneficial in stable RA, helping counter the muscle loss that comes with inflammation and steroid use. Avoid heavy loads during an acute flare and resume gradually once it settles.

/guides/benefits-pip.bodyHtml:
Benefits and Financial Support for Arthritis in the UK

Living with arthritis can have a significant financial impact. Reduced working hours, early retirement, the cost of medications, travel to appointments, home adaptations and specialist equipment all place financial strain on individuals and families. Yet many people with arthritis in the UK are unaware of the benefits and financial support they may be entitled to.

According to Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis), 1 in 4 people with musculoskeletal conditions who are eligible for benefits are not claiming them. This guide explains every major benefit available, with a particular focus on Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the primary disability benefit for working-age adults in England and Wales.

Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

PIP is a tax-free, non-means-tested benefit designed to help with the extra costs of living with a long-term health condition or disability. It is available to people aged 16 to State Pension age in England and Wales (replaced by Adult Disability Payment in Scotland). Importantly, PIP is available whether you work or not — it is not an out-of-work benefit.

PIP components and rates (2026/27)

PIP has two components, and you can claim either or both:

Daily Living Component — for help with everyday tasks like preparing food, washing, dressing, managing medications and communicating:

  • Standard rate: £76.70 per week
  • Enhanced rate: £114.60 per week

Confirm current amounts on GOV.UK PIP rates.

Mobility Component — for help getting around:

  • Standard rate: £30.30 per week
  • Enhanced rate: £80.00 per week

At the enhanced rate for both components, PIP provides up to £194.60 per week (usually paid every 4 weeks), which can make a transformative difference to quality of life.

Who Is Eligible?

To qualify for PIP, you must:

  • Be aged 16 to State Pension age
  • Have a health condition or disability that has affected you for at least 3 months and is expected to continue for at least 9 months
  • Have difficulty with daily living activities and/or mobility due to your condition
  • Be resident in England or Wales (Scotland has Adult Disability Payment)

PIP eligibility depends on the daily living and mobility criteria, not the diagnosis alone. Explain how your ability varies over time and whether you can complete activities safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and within a reasonable time. The rules consider how often each difficulty occurs, including a more-than-50%-of-days test over the relevant period. Read the official assessment criteria or ask a welfare-rights adviser.

PIP Activities and Descriptors

PIP is assessed across 12 activities — 10 for daily living and 2 for mobility. Each activity has a set of descriptors worth 0–12 points. You need:

  • 8 points for the standard rate of either component
  • 12 points for the enhanced rate of either component

Daily Living Activities:

  1. Preparing food — can you chop, peel, use a cooker safely? Arthritis affecting hands/wrists is very relevant
  2. Taking nutrition — can you cut food and lift cups/utensils to your mouth?
  3. Managing therapy or monitoring a health condition — includes managing medications, doing prescribed exercises, attending appointments
  4. Washing and bathing — can you wash your body, get in/out of a bath or shower?
  5. Managing toilet needs — relevant if hip, knee or hand arthritis affects this
  6. Dressing and undressing — can you do buttons, zips, put on socks/shoes?
  7. Communicating verbally — generally less relevant for arthritis unless fatigue/pain affects concentration
  8. Reading and understanding signs — may be relevant if brain fog or medication side effects affect cognition
  9. Engaging with other people face to face — relevant if depression/anxiety from chronic pain affects social interaction
  10. Making budgeting decisions — relevant if cognitive effects of pain/fatigue affect decision-making

Mobility Activities:

  1. Planning and following journeys — relevant if pain/fatigue affects your ability to plan or cope with travel
  2. Moving around — can you stand and then move more than 200 metres, 50 metres, 20 metres? This is the key mobility descriptor for arthritis

How to Apply for PIP

  1. Call the PIP new claims line: 0800 917 2222 (Monday–Friday, 8am–5pm). You will be asked basic details and sent a "How your disability affects you" questionnaire (PIP2 form)
  2. Complete the PIP2 form: This is the most important stage. Describe typical days, better days and worse days, including how often each occurs. Explain what you cannot do, what causes pain, what takes longer, and where you need help or use aids. Be specific: "I cannot grip a kettle safely due to hand pain and stiffness" rather than "I have difficulty in the kitchen"
  3. Gather supporting evidence: Attach letters from your GP, rheumatologist, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or consultant. Include medication lists, clinic letters and any photos of swollen joints or hand deformities
  4. Attend a face-to-face or telephone assessment: An independent healthcare professional (usually a nurse or physiotherapist working for contractors like Capita or Atos) will assess your needs. Explain your difficulties and their frequency honestly
  5. Receive your decision: Decisions typically take 8–16 weeks. If awarded, PIP is usually granted for a fixed period (1–10 years) and then reviewed

Tips for a Successful PIP Claim

  • Describe fluctuation accurately — include better and worse days, their frequency, and the help, time and aids needed
  • Mention variability — arthritis is a fluctuating condition; explain how bad days differ from good days
  • Include fatigue — chronic fatigue is a major feature of inflammatory arthritis and counts toward daily living activities
  • Mention pain — describe the type, intensity and impact of pain on each activity
  • Note time taken — if a task takes you twice as long as someone without arthritis, this counts
  • List all aids and adaptations — jar openers, perching stools, grab rails, orthotics, walking sticks, wheelchairs
  • Keep a pain diary — a printable PIP evidence diary can help you record daily symptoms and prepare for a claim
  • Get help completing the form — Citizens Advice, Arthritis UK and local welfare rights services offer free support

If Your PIP Claim Is Refused

If you disagree with the decision, you have the right to challenge it:

  1. Mandatory Reconsideration — request this within 1 month of the decision. Provide additional evidence. Around 17% of reconsiderations result in a changed decision (DWP, 2024)
  2. Appeal to a tribunal — if reconsideration fails, appeal to the Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within 1 month. You'll have a hearing before an independent panel. Around 70% of PIP appeals are successful (Ministry of Justice, 2024), so it is well worth pursuing if you believe your needs were underestimated

Free help with appeals is available from Citizens Advice, law centres, and Arthritis UK (helpline: 0800 5200 520).

Other Benefits You May Be Entitled To

Attendance Allowance

If you are over State Pension age, Attendance Allowance replaces PIP. It has two rates:

  • Lower rate: £76.70 per week (daytime or night-time needs)
  • Higher rate: £114.60 per week (day and night needs)

There is no mobility component, but qualifying opens access to additional benefits like Pension Credit, Council Tax Reduction and Carer's Allowance for someone who helps you.

Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

If arthritis prevents you from working and you have enough National Insurance contributions, you may qualify for New Style ESA. This provides:

  • Rates depend on age and assessment group; check current ESA rates
  • Payment duration depends on the applicable assessment group and benefit rules

Universal Credit

If you have limited income and savings, Universal Credit may provide additional financial support. If you have a Limited Capability for Work and Work-Related Activity (LCWRA) determination, an additional amount may apply. The amount depends on the current rules and your circumstances; check GOV.UK rather than relying on an old quoted rate. PIP does not automatically establish LCWRA entitlement: Universal Credit uses its own rules and assessment process. Check current Universal Credit guidance and get advice about your circumstances.

Carer's Allowance

If someone provides care for you for at least 35 hours per week and you receive either rate of the daily living component of PIP (or another qualifying benefit, such as Attendance Allowance), your carer may be eligible for Carer's Allowance subject to earnings and other eligibility conditions. Check the current eligibility rules; Scotland uses Carer Support Payment.

Blue Badge Scheme

The Blue Badge allows you to park closer to your destination. Blue Badge eligibility depends on the qualifying criteria and the rules in your nation; receiving enhanced PIP mobility is not a complete description of those rules. Check official Blue Badge guidance and your council’s criteria. You can also apply via your local council if you have a condition that affects your ability to walk, even if you don't receive PIP mobility.

Apply through your local council — the process typically takes 6–12 weeks.

Motability Scheme

If you receive the enhanced rate mobility component of PIP, you can use it to lease a car, powered wheelchair or scooter through the Motability Scheme. You exchange some or all of your mobility payment for a vehicle, with insurance, servicing, breakdown cover and adaptations included. Over 640,000 people in the UK use Motability.

Disabled Facilities Grant

Local authorities provide grants of up to £30,000 (England) for home adaptations such as:

  • Walk-in showers and level-access bathrooms
  • Stair lifts
  • Ramps and widened doorways
  • Kitchen modifications

Apply through your local council. An occupational therapist assessment is usually required.

Council Tax Reduction

If you receive PIP or Attendance Allowance, you may be eligible for a Council Tax reduction or exemption. Some councils also offer a disability reduction scheme if your property has been adapted (e.g., an extra bathroom). Contact your local council to check eligibility.

Prescription Charge Exemptions

In England, if you meet certain criteria you may be exempt from prescription charges:

  • If you receive certain benefits (income-based ESA, Universal Credit below threshold)
  • If you have a medical exemption certificate (currently limited to specific conditions — arthritis alone does not qualify, but some related conditions do)
  • If you are over 60 or under 16 (or under 19 in full-time education)
  • A Prescription Prepayment Certificate (£111.60/year) covers unlimited prescriptions and saves money if you have 12+ items per year

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland provide free prescriptions for all residents.

Your Rights at Work

Under the Equality Act 2010, arthritis is likely to qualify as a disability if it has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on your ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. This means your employer must make reasonable adjustments, which could include:

  • Flexible working hours or home working
  • Ergonomic workstation adaptations
  • Modified duties during flare-ups
  • Extra breaks
  • Reserved parking close to the entrance
  • Time off for medical appointments

Access to Work is a government scheme that can fund workplace adjustments costing more than what's reasonable for the employer — including specialist equipment, support workers and taxi fares. Read our Access to Work library guide, apply through GOV.UK or call 0800 121 7479.

Where to Get Free Help

  • Citizens Advice — free benefits advice and form-filling help: citizensadvice.org.uk or 0800 144 8848
  • Arthritis UK helpline (formerly Versus Arthritis) — 0800 5200 520 (includes benefits advice)
  • Turn2us — benefits calculator and grants directory: turn2us.org.uk
  • Scope — disability rights and benefits support: scope.org.uk
  • Local welfare rights services — many councils offer free benefits advice
  • NRAS — National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society: nras.org.uk
  • GOV.UK — official PIP information: gov.uk/pip

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide is based on GOV.UK official benefit rates and eligibility criteria (2026/27 GOV.UK rates), DWP statistics, Ministry of Justice tribunal statistics, and guidance from Citizens Advice and Arthritis UK. Benefit rates are subject to annual uprating (usually in April). This information is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal or financial advice. For personalised advice, contact Citizens Advice or a qualified welfare rights adviser.

faqs.q: How do I claim PIP for arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: Call the PIP new claims line on 0800 917 2222 (or claim via GOV.UK where available), complete the 'How your disability affects you' (PIP2) form describing better and worse days and how often difficulties occur, attach GP/rheumatology evidence, attend the assessment, then wait for the decision. Keep a symptom diary — Living With Arthritis offers a free PIP evidence diary at /resources/pip-evidence-diary. This is educational guidance only; always check https://www.gov.uk/pip and get regulated welfare advice for your own claim.

faqs.q: How much is PIP for arthritis in 2026/27?
faqs.a: From April 2026 (GOV.UK rates): Daily Living is £76.70/week (standard) or £114.60/week (enhanced); Mobility is £30.30/week (standard) or £80.00/week (enhanced). You can get either or both. The maximum (both enhanced) is £194.60/week, usually paid every 4 weeks. Rates are uprated each April — always check gov.uk/pip.

faqs.q: Can I claim PIP for osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes — PIP is not diagnosis-led. Assessors look at how arthritis affects daily living and mobility across better and worse days, considering the reliability and frequency rules (points for activities such as cooking, dressing, managing treatments and moving around). Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and other forms can all qualify if the functional impact is enough.

faqs.q: How long must arthritis have affected me before I claim PIP?
faqs.a: Your difficulties must have lasted at least 3 months and be expected to continue for at least 9 months. You usually need to be aged 16 to State Pension age and living in England or Wales (Scotland uses Adult Disability Payment; Northern Ireland has a separate PIP system).

faqs.q: What if my PIP claim for arthritis is refused?
faqs.a: Ask for a Mandatory Reconsideration within 1 month and send stronger evidence (rheumatology letters, OT/physio notes, a diary covering better and worse days). If that fails, appeal to the Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within 1 month — a large share of PIP appeals succeed. Free help is available from Citizens Advice and welfare rights services.

faqs.q: What replaces PIP after State Pension age?
faqs.a: Attendance Allowance is the main disability benefit if you claim after State Pension age (it has no mobility component). From April 2026 GOV.UK rates: lower £76.70/week and higher £114.60/week. If you already get PIP when you reach State Pension age, PIP can often continue — check GOV.UK or a benefits adviser before stopping a claim.

faqs.q: Where can I get free help with a PIP form for arthritis?
faqs.a: Citizens Advice, local welfare rights / law centres, and disability charities can help with PIP2 forms and appeals. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) runs a helpline on 0800 5200 520. Living With Arthritis (charity 1218461) publishes this guide for education only — we are independent of Arthritis UK and cannot replace regulated advice.

faqs.q: Does PIP affect other benefits or mean-tested support?
faqs.a: PIP itself is not means-tested and is usually ignored as income for Universal Credit, but it can unlock premiums, Blue Badge eligibility routes, Motability (enhanced mobility) and carer entitlement. Always check a benefits calculator (e.g. Turn2us or Entitledto) or an adviser for your household.

faqs.q: Can I work while claiming PIP for arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. PIP is not an out-of-work benefit — you can work full-time, part-time or not at all if you meet the daily living or mobility criteria. Tell DWP if your needs change a lot, and ask your employer about Equality Act reasonable adjustments and Access to Work support.

faqs.q: How should I describe arthritis flares on the PIP form?
faqs.a: Describe better and worse days and how often each happens. Cover morning stiffness, pain, fatigue, extra time needed, aids you use, and what you cannot do safely or repeatedly (for example gripping a kettle or walking on a flare day). A short symptom diary helps — use our free printable PIP evidence diary at /resources/pip-evidence-diary.

faqs.q: What if I live in Scotland — is PIP different?
faqs.a: In Scotland, working-age adults claim Adult Disability Payment (ADP) from Social Security Scotland instead of PIP. If you move between Scotland and England or Wales, report the move and claim the correct benefit so payments are not interrupted — check mygov.scot for ADP and GOV.UK for PIP.

/guides/knee-replacement-surgery.bodyHtml:
A Patient's Guide to Knee Replacement Surgery

Knee replacement — known clinically as knee arthroplasty — is one of the most successful and well-studied operations performed in the UK. Around 110,000 knee replacements are carried out each year in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (National Joint Registry, 2023), and the great majority of patients report substantial pain relief and improved mobility within a year of surgery.

This guide walks you through every stage of the patient journey: deciding whether surgery is right for you, what to expect in hospital, how to prepare your home, and the realities of recovery. It is written for UK patients and reflects current NICE guidance (NG226) and Royal College of Surgeons standards.

When to Consider Knee Replacement

Knee replacement is recommended when conservative treatments no longer control pain and disability. Typical triggers include:

  • Pain that disturbs sleep — waking at night or being unable to find a comfortable position
  • Reduced walking distance — struggling to walk for more than 20–30 minutes
  • Difficulty with stairs, getting out of a chair, or driving
  • Persistent stiffness and visible deformity (bow-leg or knock-knee)
  • X-ray evidence of advanced arthritis — narrowed joint space, bone spurs, bone-on-bone contact
  • Symptoms not improving after 3–6 months of weight loss, physiotherapy, analgesia and (where appropriate) steroid injections

If these apply, ask your GP for an orthopaedic referral. You may also want to read our companion guide on knee arthritis and managing the wait for surgery.

Types of Knee Replacement

Total Knee Replacement (TKR)

The whole joint surface is replaced — the lower end of the femur, the top of the tibia, and usually the underside of the patella. TKR accounts for around 90% of UK knee replacements. Implants are typically cobalt-chromium and polyethylene, fixed with bone cement.

Partial (Unicompartmental) Knee Replacement

Only the damaged compartment (usually the inner side) is resurfaced. Recovery is faster and the knee feels more "natural", but it suits only around 1 in 4 patients — those with arthritis confined to one compartment and intact ligaments.

Patellofemoral Replacement

Resurfaces only the kneecap and its groove. Used for isolated kneecap arthritis — about 1–2% of cases.

Revision Knee Replacement

A second operation if the original implant loosens, wears out or becomes infected. Revisions are technically harder, take longer to recover from, and are best done in specialist centres.

Preparing for Surgery (Prehabilitation)

"Prehab" — getting fitter before surgery — has strong evidence for shorter hospital stays and faster recovery. UK enhanced recovery programmes recommend:

  • Quadriceps and glute strengthening — straight-leg raises, mini-squats, step-ups (3–4 sessions per week for 6+ weeks)
  • Aerobic conditioning — cycling, swimming, or aqua-walking
  • Weight loss — a BMI under 35 reduces complication risk; many trusts now require BMI optimisation
  • Stopping smoking at least 8 weeks before surgery — smoking doubles wound infection risk
  • Reducing alcohol to under 14 units per week
  • Optimising chronic conditions — diabetes (HbA1c < 69 mmol/mol), blood pressure, anaemia
  • Dental check-up — untreated dental infection is a known source of implant infection

You will usually attend a pre-operative assessment clinic 2–6 weeks before surgery for blood tests, ECG, MRSA swabs, and an anaesthetic review.

Preparing Your Home

A small amount of planning makes early recovery far easier:

  • Move frequently used items to waist height — no bending or reaching
  • Set up a recovery base downstairs if possible, with a firm chair (knee at 90°), footstool, and bedside table
  • Remove trip hazards — loose rugs, trailing cables, clutter on stairs
  • Buy or borrow a raised toilet seat, long-handled shoe horn, sock aid, grabber and shower stool
  • Batch-cook and freeze meals for the first 2–3 weeks
  • Arrange help with shopping, pets, laundry and childcare for at least 2 weeks
  • Tell family you will not be driving for around 6 weeks

What Happens in Hospital

Most UK hospital trusts now follow an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathway. A typical timeline:

Day of Surgery

You arrive fasted (usually from midnight, or as instructed). Anaesthetic is most often spinal with sedation, which is associated with less blood loss and quicker recovery than general anaesthesia. Surgery takes 60–90 minutes. You are encouraged to stand and walk within a few hours with a physiotherapist.

Days 1–2

Pain is managed with regular paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory if suitable, and short-term opioids. You will practise walking with crutches or a frame, climbing stairs, and bending the knee. Most patients are discharged within 1–3 days, some on the same day under modern ERAS protocols.

Before Discharge

You will be given blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2–4 weeks to reduce clot risk, a clear exercise sheet, contact numbers, and a follow-up appointment for around 6 weeks.

Recovery Timeline: Week by Week

Recovery is gradual. The pattern below is typical but individual — your surgical team's advice always takes priority.

Weeks 1–2: Pain & Swelling Control

  • Walk short distances with crutches every 1–2 hours
  • Ice the knee for 15–20 minutes, 4–6 times daily
  • Elevate the leg above heart level when resting
  • Do the prescribed exercises 3–4 times daily — quad sets, ankle pumps, heel slides
  • Aim for knee bend (flexion) of 70–90° by the end of week 2

Weeks 3–6: Building Movement

  • Progress to one crutch, then walking unaided indoors
  • Target flexion of 100–110° and full extension (straight knee)
  • Begin stationary cycling on low resistance once you have 100° of bend
  • 6-week orthopaedic review — surgeon checks wound, range of movement and X-rays
  • Most patients can return to driving once they can do an emergency stop comfortably (typically 6 weeks for a right knee)

Weeks 6–12: Strength & Confidence

  • Return to desk-based work, light shopping, social activities
  • Add resistance training, swimming, and longer walks
  • Swelling around the knee is normal for several more months

Months 3–12: Long-Term Recovery

  • Steady improvement in pain, strength and stamina
  • Return to recommended activities: walking, cycling, swimming, golf, doubles tennis, gentle hiking
  • Avoid high-impact activities — running, contact sport, jumping — which shorten implant life
  • Full recovery is usually reached between 6 and 12 months

Essential Recovery Exercises

These exercises should be done daily from day 1 unless your physiotherapist advises otherwise. See our full exercise hub for more progressions.

  • Quad sets — tighten the thigh muscle and push the back of the knee into the bed for 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Ankle pumps — move feet up and down to reduce clot risk, 20 reps every hour
  • Heel slides — slide the heel towards the buttock to bend the knee, 10 reps
  • Straight-leg raise — with knee locked straight, lift the leg 20 cm, hold 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Seated knee extension — sit on a firm chair, straighten the knee fully, hold 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Standing knee bends — holding a worktop, bend the operated knee back behind you, 10 reps

Risks and How They Are Managed

Serious complications are uncommon but worth understanding. UK National Joint Registry data show:

  • Deep infection — around 1 in 100. Risk reduced by antibiotics at induction, laminar-flow theatres and good blood sugar control.
  • Blood clots (DVT / PE) — around 1 in 100 symptomatic, reduced by early mobilisation and post-op anticoagulants.
  • Stiffness requiring manipulation under anaesthetic — around 2–3%.
  • Nerve or blood-vessel injury — under 1%.
  • Persistent pain — 15–20% of patients report ongoing discomfort at 1 year; usually mild and manageable.
  • Implant loosening or wear — gradual; most implants last 20–25 years.
  • Death within 90 days — under 0.5%, mostly from cardiovascular events.

Risk is higher in patients who smoke, have a BMI above 40, or have poorly controlled diabetes, heart or kidney disease. Your surgical team will discuss your individual risk before consent.

Public Waiting Lists and Private Options

Knee replacement is a routine UK operation. Under the UK 18-week referral-to-treatment standard you have the right to be treated within 18 weeks of referral. If your local trust cannot meet this, you can ask to be transferred to another public or publicly funded independent provider — this is sometimes called the "right to choose".

Private knee replacement in the UK typically costs £12,000–£16,000 all-inclusive. Patients often choose private care to shorten waits or to select a specific consultant. Outcomes are similar to public care when the same surgeon and implant are used. See our guide on managing the UK waiting list for practical steps while you wait.

Alternatives and Delaying Surgery

Many patients can delay or avoid surgery with a structured non-surgical plan. NICE recommends offering all patients with knee osteoarthritis a combined approach before considering surgery:

  • Weight management — losing 5–10% of body weight reduces knee pain as much as some surgical interventions
  • Structured exercise — supervised physiotherapy for 6–12 weeks; ESCAPE-pain is a UK programme proven to reduce pain by 30–50%
