  • Topical NSAID gels (ibuprofen or diclofenac) — first-line analgesia under NICE NG226
  • Oral analgesia — paracetamol, short courses of oral NSAIDs with gastric protection
  • Intra-articular steroid injections — short-term pain relief lasting 4–12 weeks
  • Walking aids — a stick used in the opposite hand can reduce knee load by 25%
  • An anti-inflammatory Mediterranean diet to reduce systemic inflammation and aid weight loss

Newer treatments — PRP (platelet-rich plasma), hyaluronic acid injections and stem-cell therapy — have limited or inconsistent evidence and are not routinely funded by the UK health service.

The Emotional Side of Surgery

Major surgery can be daunting. Anxiety, low mood and sleep disturbance are common before and after the operation. Patients often describe a "third-week dip" when the initial momentum fades and progress feels slow. This is normal. Recovery is rarely linear. Things that help:

  • Setting small weekly goals — bending 5° more, walking 5 minutes longer
  • Keeping a brief daily diary of pain, swelling and movement
  • Staying socially connected — visitors, video calls, the Living With Arthritis community
  • Speaking to your GP early if low mood persists beyond 2–3 weeks

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide draws on NICE guideline NG226 (Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management), the UK National Joint Registry 20th Annual Report (2023), Royal College of Surgeons of England commissioning guidance for knee replacement, British Orthopaedic Association enhanced recovery standards, and Cochrane reviews of prehabilitation and post-operative physiotherapy. It is for general education and does not replace personalised advice from your GP, surgeon or physiotherapist.

faqs.q: When should I consider knee replacement surgery?
faqs.a: Knee replacement is usually considered when severe osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis causes daily pain that disturbs sleep, limits walking under 30 minutes, and has not responded to at least 3–6 months of non-surgical treatment (weight loss, physiotherapy, painkillers, steroid injections). NICE guidance (NG226) recommends referral when symptoms substantially affect quality of life.

faqs.q: How long does a knee replacement last?
faqs.a: Modern total knee replacements last around 20–25 years in 80–90% of patients, according to the UK National Joint Registry. Longevity depends on age at surgery, weight, activity level and implant type. Younger, more active patients may need revision surgery later in life.

faqs.q: How long is recovery from knee replacement surgery ?
faqs.a: Most patients are discharged within 1–3 days. You can usually walk with crutches within 24 hours, drive at 6 weeks, and return to desk work at 6–8 weeks. Full recovery — including swelling reduction and maximum strength — typically takes 6–12 months. Daily physiotherapy exercises are essential during this period.

faqs.q: What is the UK waiting list for a knee replacement?
faqs.a: As of 2024, the median public-system wait for a knee replacement in England is around 18–22 weeks from referral, though some trusts exceed 40 weeks. You have the legal right under the UK 18-week referral-to-treatment standard to be treated within 18 weeks of referral and can request alternative providers if waits exceed this.

faqs.q: What are the risks of knee replacement surgery?
faqs.a: Serious complications are uncommon. Around 1 in 100 patients develop a deep infection, 1 in 100 a blood clot (DVT or pulmonary embolism), and 1 in 200 nerve damage. About 15–20% of patients have residual pain or stiffness. Mortality within 90 days is under 0.5%. Risks rise with age, obesity, smoking and uncontrolled diabetes.

faqs.q: Can I avoid knee replacement surgery?
faqs.a: Many patients delay or avoid surgery by combining weight loss (every 1 kg lost reduces knee load by 4 kg per step), quadriceps strengthening, low-impact exercise (swimming, cycling), an anti-inflammatory Mediterranean diet, and a stepped pain plan (paracetamol, topical NSAIDs, injections). However, end-stage arthritis with bone-on-bone changes rarely responds long-term to conservative care.

/guides/steroids-for-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Steroids for arthritis: an overview

Corticosteroids — often shortened to "steroids" — are one of the most widely used treatments for inflammatory joint pain. They are synthetic versions of cortisol, a hormone the body produces naturally, and they work by switching off the chemical signals that cause inflammation, swelling and pain.

In arthritis care, steroids are used in three main ways: as injections into a joint (intra-articular), as short courses of tablets (oral), and occasionally as an intramuscular injection for a body-wide effect. Each route has a different role, and choosing the right one depends on the type of arthritis, which joints are affected, and how long-lasting the relief needs to be.

Steroids do not slow the underlying disease in osteoarthritis, and they are not a long-term solution. What they offer is a window of relief — often enough to get someone moving, sleeping, exercising or completing physiotherapy that would otherwise be impossible because of pain.

How steroids work in an inflamed joint

In a healthy joint, the synovial lining produces a small amount of lubricating fluid. In inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout) and during osteoarthritis flares, this lining becomes thickened and produces excess fluid loaded with inflammatory chemicals — prostaglandins, cytokines and white blood cells.

A steroid injection delivers a concentrated dose directly into this inflamed tissue. Within hours it begins to:

  • Block the production of inflammatory prostaglandins
  • Reduce the number of immune cells in the joint
  • Shrink the swollen synovial lining
  • Lower the volume of excess joint fluid

The result is less pressure inside the joint capsule, less mechanical pain, and often a noticeable improvement in range of movement.

Types of steroid injection

The three corticosteroids most commonly used in UK arthritis clinics are:

  • Methylprednisolone (Depo-Medrone) — medium-acting, widely used for knees, shoulders and hips
  • Triamcinolone (Kenalog) — longer-acting, often used for larger joints and tendon sheaths
  • Hydrocortisone — shorter-acting, sometimes used in smaller joints like fingers

The injection is usually mixed with a small dose of local anaesthetic (lidocaine), which gives almost immediate but brief pain relief while the steroid begins to work over the following 24–72 hours.

What to expect during a joint injection

A joint injection takes about 10–15 minutes from start to finish. You can drive yourself home afterwards. Here is what typically happens:

  • The clinician examines the joint and marks the injection site
  • The skin is cleaned with antiseptic
  • A fine needle is inserted into the joint space (sometimes guided by ultrasound)
  • If excess fluid is present, it may be drawn off first (aspiration)
  • The steroid and local anaesthetic mixture is injected
  • A small plaster is applied; you rest the joint for 24–48 hours

It is common to feel a brief sharp pressure as the needle enters the joint. Most people describe it as uncomfortable rather than painful.

Side effects and risks

Steroid injections are generally safe when given correctly and not used too often. The most common side effects are mild and short-lived:

  • Post-injection flare — a temporary increase in pain for 24–48 hours, experienced by 1 in 20 people
  • Facial flushing — warmth and redness lasting a day or two
  • Raised blood sugar — important if you have diabetes; monitor closely for 3–5 days
  • Skin changes — thinning or loss of pigment at the injection site (more visible in darker skin)
  • Mood or sleep disturbance — brief and self-limiting

Rare but more serious risks include joint infection (less than 1 in 10,000), tendon weakening if injected too close to a tendon, and accelerated cartilage loss with repeated injections. This is why most clinicians limit injections to a maximum of 3–4 per joint per year.

Oral steroids and inflammatory arthritis

For people with rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, lupus or vasculitis, short courses of oral steroids — usually prednisolone — are a standard part of treatment. They are used as a "bridge" to control inflammation rapidly while slower disease-modifying drugs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, biologics) take effect over 6–12 weeks.

Typical regimens range from a short tapering course over a few weeks to longer maintenance doses in conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica, which may need treatment for 1–2 years.

Long-term oral steroids carry meaningful risks — weight gain, raised blood pressure, osteoporosis, increased infection risk and changes to blood sugar control. Anyone taking prednisolone for more than 3 months should be assessed for bone protection (calcium, vitamin D and often a bisphosphonate) under NICE guidance.

Steroids for osteoarthritis: what the evidence says

NICE guidance (NG226, 2022) lists intra-articular steroid injections as an option for osteoarthritis when other measures have not controlled symptoms. Cochrane reviews show short-term pain relief of 4–8 weeks for knee osteoarthritis, with less convincing evidence for hip and hand osteoarthritis.

Steroids do not slow cartilage loss in osteoarthritis, and there is some evidence that frequent repeat injections (more than 4 per year in the same joint) may accelerate it. For this reason they are best used strategically — to break a flare-up cycle, to enable physiotherapy, or to bridge the wait for joint replacement surgery — rather than as a routine treatment.

Alternatives to steroid injections

Steroids are one option among several. Depending on your joint, your diagnosis and your goals, your clinician may discuss:

  • Hyaluronic acid injections — sometimes offered for knee osteoarthritis, though NICE no longer routinely recommends them on the public health service
  • Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) — privately available; evidence is mixed and improving
  • Topical NSAIDs — diclofenac or ibuprofen gels are first-line for hand and knee osteoarthritis
  • Oral pain relief — paracetamol, short courses of oral NSAIDs with stomach protection
  • Strengthening exercise and weight management — the strongest evidence base for long-term improvement in osteoarthritis
  • Disease-modifying drugs (DMARDs) — for inflammatory arthritis, the foundation of long-term control

How to access steroid treatment in the UK

Steroid injections and short courses of oral steroids are available free through the public health service. The most common routes are:

  • Your GP — many GPs are trained to inject knees, shoulders and the base of the thumb
  • First Contact Physiotherapists — increasingly trained as independent prescribers and joint injectors; bookable without a GP referral
  • Rheumatology clinics — for inflammatory arthritis and complex small-joint injections
  • Orthopaedic outpatients — when injections are part of a surgical pathway
  • Musculoskeletal interface services — local triage clinics that can inject larger joints quickly

Private steroid injections typically cost £150–£300 per joint and are available through physiotherapy clinics, MSK specialists and private rheumatologists if you need faster access.

Questions to ask your clinician

  • How long is this injection likely to last for me?
  • What is the realistic chance it will help?
  • How many injections have I had in this joint, and is another safe?
  • What should I do — and avoid — in the 48 hours after the injection?
  • How will this affect my diabetes / blood pressure / other medication?
  • Are there alternatives I should consider first?
  • What is the plan if this injection doesn't work?

Key takeaways

  • Steroids reduce inflammation; they don't cure arthritis or repair cartilage.
  • Injections work best when used strategically — to break a flare or enable rehabilitation — not as a long-term routine.
  • Limit injections to 3–4 per joint per year to protect cartilage.
  • Oral steroids are essential in inflammatory arthritis but need bone-protection planning if used long-term.
  • Available free through GPs, First Contact Physios and rheumatology on the public health service.
  • Always pair steroid treatment with exercise, weight management and disease-modifying therapy where appropriate.

faqs.q: What is a steroid injection for arthritis?
faqs.a: A steroid (corticosteroid) injection delivers a small dose of synthetic cortisone directly into an inflamed joint or the soft tissue around it. The medication dampens the inflammation that causes pain, swelling and stiffness — typically giving relief that lasts a few weeks to several months. Common drugs used include methylprednisolone, triamcinolone and hydrocortisone.

faqs.q: How long does a steroid injection last for joint pain?
faqs.a: Most people feel improvement within 24–72 hours. Pain relief typically lasts 6 weeks to 6 months, depending on the joint, the severity of inflammation and the type of arthritis. Knees and shoulders often respond well; smaller joints in the hands may give shorter relief.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of steroids for arthritis?
faqs.a: Short-term: a temporary flare of pain in the first 24–48 hours, facial flushing, raised blood sugar (especially in people with diabetes), mild mood changes and skin thinning or pigment change at the injection site. Long-term or repeated use can weaken cartilage, increase infection risk, cause weight gain, osteoporosis and high blood pressure. This is why injections are usually limited to 3–4 per joint per year.

faqs.q: Are steroid tablets used for arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. Oral steroids such as prednisolone are commonly used as a short-term 'bridge' in inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, lupus) while slower-acting disease-modifying drugs take effect. They are not routinely used for osteoarthritis because the risks of long-term oral steroids outweigh the benefits.

faqs.q: Can I get a steroid injection on the public health service?
faqs.a: Yes. Steroid injections are available free through GPs trained in joint injections, First Contact Physiotherapists, rheumatology clinics and orthopaedic services. Waiting times vary from same-week (GP) to several months (hospital outpatient).

faqs.q: How often can I have steroid injections?
faqs.a: Most clinicians limit injections to a maximum of 3–4 per joint per year, with at least 3 months between injections in the same joint. Repeated frequent injections can accelerate cartilage damage in osteoarthritis.

faqs.q: Do steroid injections work for osteoarthritis of the knee?
faqs.a: Evidence shows steroid injections give short-term pain relief (typically 4–8 weeks) for knee osteoarthritis, particularly during flare-ups. NICE guidance (NG226) supports their use as an option when conservative treatment hasn't controlled symptoms, but they should not be the first or only treatment.

/guides/azathioprine-for-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Azathioprine for arthritis: an overview

Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) that has been used in UK rheumatology for more than 50 years. It works by quietening an overactive immune system — the underlying problem in lupus, vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis and several other inflammatory conditions — rather than just masking pain.

It is rarely the first DMARD tried in rheumatoid arthritis (methotrexate is), but it is a mainstay treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), vasculitis, autoimmune hepatitis-associated arthritis, and as a steroid-sparing option when long-term prednisolone is causing problems. It is also widely used in inflammatory bowel disease, where joint involvement is common.

Azathioprine works slowly — most people notice improvement at 8–12 weeks and full benefit by 3–6 months — so it is usually started alongside a short course of oral steroid that controls symptoms while the DMARD builds up.

How azathioprine works

Azathioprine is a "prodrug": once swallowed, the body converts it to 6-mercaptopurine, which interferes with the building blocks (purines) that immune cells need to multiply. By slowing the production of the most active lymphocytes, it dampens down the autoimmune attack on joints, kidneys, blood vessels and other tissues.

Because it suppresses immune cell turnover rather than blocking a single inflammatory signal, azathioprine is broadly active across many autoimmune conditions — but the same mechanism is why blood monitoring is essential.

Conditions azathioprine is used for

  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) — first- or second-line steroid-sparing agent, particularly for joint, skin and mild kidney involvement
  • Vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, polyarteritis nodosa) — used for maintenance after remission is induced
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — when methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide are unsuitable
  • Inflammatory bowel disease with arthritis — treats both gut and joint disease
  • Autoimmune hepatitis with joint symptoms
  • Polymyositis and dermatomyositis — as a steroid-sparing agent
  • BehÃ§et's disease with arthritis or uveitis

Before you start: TPMT testing and baseline checks

UK rheumatology shared-care guidance requires several checks before the first dose:

  • TPMT enzyme test — a single blood test that identifies the small number of people who break azathioprine down too slowly and are at high risk of toxicity
  • Full blood count (FBC) — baseline white cells, haemoglobin and platelets
  • Liver function tests (LFTs) — baseline ALT, AST and bilirubin
  • Urea and electrolytes (U&Es) — kidney function
  • Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV screen — to avoid reactivating hidden infections
  • Varicella (chickenpox) immunity check — vaccination may be needed before starting
  • Up-to-date pneumococcal and annual flu vaccines — give before starting where possible

If your TPMT activity is low, your specialist will start at a much lower dose or choose a different DMARD. If it is absent, azathioprine should not be used.

How azathioprine is taken

Azathioprine is taken as tablets (common tablet strengths include 25 mg and 50 mg). Rheumatology teams individualise the dose using body weight, TPMT status, blood results and the condition being treated — often referring to BNF / BSR shared-care ranges. Your rheumatology team will set your dose; never change it without specialist advice, and do not calculate a dose from this page.

Practical tips:

  • Take with or just after food to reduce nausea
  • Ask your team whether splitting the daily dose helps if a single dose causes stomach upset
  • Take it at the same time each day so it's easy to remember
  • Don't crush or break the tablets — wash your hands after handling
  • Store at room temperature, away from children

Blood-test monitoring on azathioprine

Regular monitoring is what makes long-term azathioprine safe. A typical UK shared-care schedule looks like this:

  • Weeks 0–6: FBC and LFTs every 1–2 weeks while the dose is being increased
  • Months 2–3: every 4 weeks
  • Long term (stable dose): every 12 weeks indefinitely
  • After any dose change: back to fortnightly bloods for 6 weeks

Your GP will usually do the bloods under a shared-care agreement with your rheumatology team. Don't skip them, even when you feel well — they pick up bone-marrow or liver problems before you would notice symptoms.

Side effects of azathioprine

Common and usually mild

  • Nausea, loss of appetite or mild stomach upset (especially in the first few weeks)
  • Mild hair thinning
  • A flu-like feeling — aches, mild fever, headache — in the first 1–2 weeks. If this is severe or persistent, contact your team; it can occasionally be a hypersensitivity reaction that means azathioprine must be stopped
  • Mouth ulcers

Less common but important

  • Bone-marrow suppression — low white cells (raised infection risk), anaemia or low platelets (easy bruising, bleeding)
  • Liver inflammation — usually picked up on routine bloods before symptoms appear
  • Pancreatitis — severe upper-abdominal pain radiating to the back; needs urgent assessment
  • Increased risk of infections — including shingles and chest infections
  • Long-term skin-cancer risk — sun protection (SPF 50, hats, covered clothing) is important; check your skin regularly
  • Small long-term increase in lymphoma risk — particularly with very long use; the absolute risk remains low and is usually outweighed by disease benefit

Contact your rheumatology team urgently if you develop fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding, severe stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or a new rash.

Drug interactions to know

  • Allopurinol (for gout) — the most dangerous interaction. It blocks the breakdown of azathioprine; the azathioprine dose must be reduced to about a quarter, or a different DMARD chosen. Tell every prescriber if you take both.
  • Febuxostat — same problem as allopurinol; avoid the combination.
  • Trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole — raise the risk of low blood counts.
  • Warfarin — INR can change; more frequent monitoring is needed.
  • ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril) — occasionally cause anaemia when combined.
  • Live vaccines (MMR, yellow fever, nasal flu, BCG, shingles Zostavax) — avoid while on azathioprine. The non-live shingles vaccine (Shingrix), inactivated flu and pneumococcal vaccines are recommended.

Azathioprine, pregnancy and breastfeeding

Azathioprine is one of the few immunosuppressants that can usually be continued safely during pregnancy and breastfeeding when the underlying condition requires ongoing treatment. Long-term registry data from women with lupus and inflammatory bowel disease show no consistent increase in major birth defects. Untreated flares of lupus or vasculitis carry significant risks to both mother and baby, so stopping azathioprine in pregnancy is usually not recommended.

Plan any pregnancy with your rheumatology team. Men taking azathioprine can father children safely; older advice to stop the drug before conception has been superseded.

Living well on azathioprine

  • Sun protection — daily SPF 50 on exposed skin, covered clothing, hat. Have any new or changing moles checked promptly.
  • Vaccinations — annual inactivated flu, pneumococcal, COVID-19 boosters and the non-live shingles vaccine (Shingrix). Avoid live vaccines.
  • Infections — contact your GP early for sore throats, chesty coughs, urinary symptoms or shingles-type rashes. Don't wait it out.
  • Alcohol — stay within 14 units per week; avoid binges. Stop completely if your liver tests rise.
  • Diet and exercise — the usual anti-inflammatory pattern (see our Diet Guide and Exercise Guide) supports general health and helps offset steroid side effects if you are also on prednisolone.
  • Travel — get pre-travel advice 6–8 weeks ahead; some destinations need vaccines that must be planned around your immunosuppression.

How azathioprine is prescribed in the UK

Azathioprine for arthritis is a specialist-initiated drug. The typical pathway is:

  • Diagnosis and decision to treat by a rheumatologist (or other relevant specialist)
  • Baseline checks, TPMT test and counselling at the rheumatology clinic
  • First few weeks of prescribing and monitoring by the specialist team
  • Once the dose is stable, prescribing handed to the GP under a shared-care agreement, with the rheumatology team still reviewing you 6–12 monthly

Shared-care arrangements mean your GP can issue repeats, do your monitoring bloods and act on results — but anything unusual (low counts, raised liver enzymes, infections, planning pregnancy) should be flagged to your specialist team.

Questions to ask your rheumatology team

  • Why is azathioprine the right DMARD for me, rather than methotrexate or another option?
  • What was my TPMT result, and how does it affect my dose?
  • What target dose are we working towards, and over how many weeks?
  • Who arranges my monitoring bloods — and what do I do if I'm called for one I can't attend?
  • Which symptoms should make me contact you urgently?
  • Which vaccines should I have, and which should I avoid?
  • What's the plan for pregnancy / fatherhood if relevant?
  • If azathioprine doesn't work or I can't tolerate it, what's the next option?

Key takeaways

  • Azathioprine is a steroid-sparing DMARD widely used in lupus, vasculitis and some forms of inflammatory arthritis.
  • It works slowly — expect 8–12 weeks for benefit, 3–6 months for full effect.
  • A TPMT blood test before starting is essential to avoid severe toxicity.
  • Regular FBC and liver-function monitoring is what makes long-term use safe.
  • The dangerous interaction to remember is allopurinol; tell every prescriber.
  • It is usually safe to continue in pregnancy and breastfeeding under specialist supervision.
  • Pair with sun protection, vaccinations, early infection care, and exercise / diet support for the best long-term outcome.

This guide is educational and does not replace advice from your rheumatology team or GP. Always follow the dose and monitoring plan your specialist has set for you. Reference standards: BNF (British National Formulary) and British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) DMARD safety guidelines.

faqs.q: What is azathioprine used for in arthritis?
faqs.a: Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant disease-modifying drug (DMARD) used to calm an overactive immune system in inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. In arthritis care it is most often prescribed for lupus (SLE), vasculitis, severe rheumatoid arthritis that hasn't responded to first-line DMARDs, and inflammatory arthritis linked to inflammatory bowel disease. It works gradually over 8–12 weeks to reduce joint inflammation, lower flare frequency and allow steroid doses to be tapered.

faqs.q: How long does azathioprine take to work?
faqs.a: Most people start to feel a reduction in joint pain, stiffness and fatigue between 8 and 12 weeks after starting treatment, with maximum benefit by 3–6 months. Because it acts slowly, it is often started alongside a short course of prednisolone (oral steroid), which controls inflammation while azathioprine builds up.

faqs.q: What is TPMT testing and why does it matter before azathioprine?
faqs.a: TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase) is an enzyme that breaks azathioprine down. About 1 in 300 people have very low or absent TPMT activity, which dramatically raises the risk of severe bone-marrow suppression. UK guidance (BNF and BSR) recommends a TPMT blood test before the first dose. People with low TPMT may need a much lower dose; those with absent TPMT should not take azathioprine at all.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of azathioprine?
faqs.a: Common, usually mild: nausea, loss of appetite, mild hair thinning and a flu-like feeling in the first few weeks. More serious risks that need monitoring include bone-marrow suppression (low white cells, anaemia, low platelets), liver inflammation, pancreatitis, increased risk of infection and a small long-term increase in risk of certain skin cancers and lymphoma. Regular blood tests are how these are picked up early.

faqs.q: How often do I need blood tests on azathioprine?
faqs.a: Typical UK rheumatology shared-care monitoring: full blood count and liver function tests every 1–2 weeks for the first 6 weeks, then every 4 weeks for 3 months, then every 12 weeks long term once the dose is stable. Your rheumatology team or GP under a shared-care agreement will arrange this.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on azathioprine?
faqs.a: Small amounts of alcohol are generally accepted, but heavy or regular drinking increases the strain on the liver — which azathioprine is already working through. UK rheumatology teams typically advise staying within 14 units per week, spread across the week, and avoiding binge drinking. If your liver tests rise, your team may ask you to stop alcohol completely.

faqs.q: Is azathioprine safe in pregnancy?
faqs.a: Azathioprine is one of the few immunosuppressants considered acceptable to continue during pregnancy and breastfeeding when the underlying condition needs it — long-term safety data from women with lupus and inflammatory bowel disease are reassuring. Stopping it can trigger flares that may harm both mother and baby. Always plan pregnancy with your rheumatology team; do not stop azathioprine without specialist advice.

faqs.q: What medications interact with azathioprine?
faqs.a: The most important interaction is with allopurinol (used for gout) — it blocks the breakdown of azathioprine and can cause severe bone-marrow toxicity. The azathioprine dose must be cut to about a quarter, or a different DMARD chosen. Other interactions: live vaccines (avoid), warfarin (dose changes), trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (raise blood-cell suppression risk), and ACE inhibitors (rare anaemia). Always tell every prescriber, including your dentist and pharmacist, that you take azathioprine.

/guides/febuxostat-for-gout.bodyHtml:
Febuxostat for gout: an overview

Gout is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis, affecting around 1 in 40 adults in the UK. It happens when uric acid in the blood rises high enough to form sharp crystals inside joints — most often the big toe, but also the ankle, knee, wrist and fingers. The body's immune response to these crystals causes the sudden, severe pain of a gout attack.

Febuxostat (sold as Adenuric in the UK and Uloric in the US) is a urate-lowering therapy: it doesn't treat the pain of an attack, but taken every day it lowers the level of uric acid in the blood, gradually dissolves the crystal deposits already in the joints, and over time prevents new attacks.

It is one of two main long-term gout medications used in the UK, the other being allopurinol. Both work by blocking xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that produces uric acid. Febuxostat is a more targeted blocker and is the recommended option when allopurinol has not worked, has caused side effects, or cannot be dosed high enough because of reduced kidney function.

How febuxostat works

Uric acid is a normal waste product made when the body breaks down purines — chemicals found in cells and in some foods. Most people clear it efficiently through the kidneys. In gout, either too much uric acid is produced, too little is excreted, or both.

Febuxostat blocks the xanthine oxidase enzyme so the body produces less uric acid in the first place. Blood levels begin to fall within 24–48 hours, and most people reach the recommended target of below 360 µmol/L (6 mg/dL) within 4–8 weeks of starting treatment.

Once uric acid is below this threshold for long enough, the crystal deposits in the joints — and the larger lumps known as tophi under the skin — slowly dissolve. This is what protects against future attacks and reverses long-term joint damage.

Who febuxostat is for

NICE guidance (TA164) recommends febuxostat for adults with chronic gout where uric acid crystal deposition has already caused damage and where allopurinol is either contraindicated or not tolerated. In practice, your GP or rheumatologist may consider febuxostat if:

  • You have had two or more gout attacks in a year
  • You have tophi (firm lumps of urate crystals under the skin)
  • You have urate kidney stones
  • You have chronic kidney disease that limits allopurinol dosing
  • You experienced a rash, raised liver enzymes or other side effects on allopurinol
  • Your uric acid level remains above target despite maximum allopurinol

How clinicians typically monitor febuxostat

UK labels and BNF summaries describe common starting strengths (often discussed as 80 mg once daily, sometimes increased toward 120 mg if uric acid remains above target). Your rheumatology team sets your dose — do not start, increase or stop febuxostat based on this educational page. Follow the SmPC / patient leaflet they give you.

Your prescriber will usually arrange:

  • A blood test for uric acid at 2–4 weeks, then every 3–6 months
  • A blood test for liver function at 2 months and then yearly
  • A discussion about flare prophylaxis with colchicine or a low-dose NSAID for the first 3–6 months

It is essential to keep taking febuxostat every day, including during a gout attack. Stopping and starting urate-lowering therapy causes the uric acid level to swing, which triggers more attacks.

Side effects and safety

Most people tolerate febuxostat well. The most common side effects are mild and short-lived:

  • Nausea, diarrhoea or stomach discomfort
  • Headache
  • Mildly raised liver enzymes on blood tests
  • A mild rash

Less common but more serious risks include:

  • Cardiovascular events — large trials have shown a small increase in heart-related events in people with established heart or vascular disease. The European Medicines Agency advises caution in this group; allopurinol is usually preferred unless not tolerated.
  • Severe skin reactions — including Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Stop the medication and seek urgent medical advice if a rash spreads or blisters appear.
  • Liver injury — rare but reported. Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or persistent abdominal pain.

Febuxostat vs allopurinol: which is better?

For most newly diagnosed gout, allopurinol is first-line: it is cheaper, has decades of safety data, and is effective for the majority. Febuxostat is reserved for the situations listed above.

Head-to-head trials show febuxostat lowers uric acid at least as effectively as allopurinol, and often faster. It does not need dose adjustment in mild-to-moderate kidney disease, which is a major practical advantage. The trade-off is the cardiovascular signal in high-risk patients and the higher prescription cost.

Lifestyle alongside febuxostat

Medication does the heavy lifting in lowering uric acid, but diet and lifestyle reduce the burden and protect kidney function:

  • Limit alcohol — especially beer (high in purines) and spirits
  • Cut sugary drinks — fructose raises uric acid as much as alcohol
  • Reduce red meat, offal and shellfish — the highest-purine foods
  • Drink 2 litres of water a day to help the kidneys clear urate
  • Lose excess weight gradually — crash dieting and fasting raise uric acid temporarily
  • Eat low-fat dairy and cherries — both associated with lower flare risk

For a full anti-inflammatory eating pattern that supports gout and other forms of arthritis, see our foods to avoid with arthritis guide.

When to seek urgent help

  • A spreading rash, blistering, or peeling skin — stop febuxostat and contact a doctor immediately.
  • Chest pain, breathlessness or signs of stroke — call 999.
  • Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or persistent right-sided abdominal pain — possible liver injury.
  • A gout attack that doesn't settle within a week on usual treatment — speak to your GP about flare control.

Key takeaways

  • Febuxostat lowers uric acid by blocking xanthine oxidase, gradually dissolving crystal deposits in joints.
  • It is used when allopurinol is not tolerated or not effective, and when kidney function limits allopurinol dosing.
  • Target uric acid is below 360 µmol/L (300 µmol/L in severe gout with tophi).
  • Take it every single day — including during a flare — and pair it with colchicine for the first 3–6 months.
  • Watch for skin reactions, liver changes and cardiovascular risk in people with established heart disease.
  • Diet, alcohol and weight management amplify the benefit but do not replace daily medication.

faqs.q: What is febuxostat used for?
faqs.a: Febuxostat (brand names Adenuric, Uloric) is a urate-lowering medication used to prevent gout attacks in adults whose uric acid levels remain high despite lifestyle measures, or who cannot tolerate allopurinol. By lowering uric acid in the blood, it gradually dissolves the crystals in joints that cause gout flares.

faqs.q: How long does febuxostat take to work?
faqs.a: Febuxostat begins lowering uric acid within 24–48 hours, but it can take 3–6 months of consistent daily dosing to dissolve existing crystal deposits in the joints. Many people experience more frequent gout flares in the first 3–6 months as the crystals shift — this does not mean the medication has failed.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of febuxostat?
faqs.a: Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, headache, raised liver enzymes and a rash. More serious risks include cardiovascular events in people with existing heart disease, severe skin reactions (Stevens–Johnson syndrome) and liver injury. Tell your prescriber immediately about chest pain, breathlessness, jaundice or a spreading rash.

faqs.q: Is febuxostat better than allopurinol?
faqs.a: For most people, allopurinol is tried first because it is cheaper and has decades of safety data. Febuxostat is used when allopurinol is not tolerated, when uric acid targets cannot be reached on maximum allopurinol, or in people with reduced kidney function where allopurinol dosing is restricted. Febuxostat is at least as effective at lowering uric acid.

faqs.q: What is the target uric acid level on febuxostat?
faqs.a: For most people the target is below 360 µmol/L (6 mg/dL). In severe gout with tophi or frequent flares, the target is lower — below 300 µmol/L (5 mg/dL) — to encourage faster crystal dissolution. Your prescriber will check blood levels at 2–4 weeks, then every 3–6 months.

faqs.q: Do I need to take colchicine with febuxostat?
faqs.a: Often, yes — but only if your rheumatology team or GP prescribes it. Starting urate-lowering treatment can trigger flares as crystals dissolve. Clinicians commonly prescribe short-term flare prophylaxis (for example colchicine or an NSAID if suitable) for the early months. Do not start or stop prophylaxis yourself.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on febuxostat?
faqs.a: Alcohol — especially beer and spirits — raises uric acid and provokes gout flares. Febuxostat will still work, but heavy drinking undermines the treatment and increases pressure on the liver. Moderate wine intake is the lowest-risk choice; staying within 14 UK units per week is sensible.

/guides/painkillers-and-nsaids.bodyHtml:
Painkillers and NSAIDs for arthritis: an overview

Painkillers are the most widely used treatments for arthritis in the UK — and the most widely misunderstood. The right medication, at the right dose, for the right length of time can transform daily life. The wrong one, used for too long, can cause stomach bleeding, kidney damage and avoidable cardiovascular events.

This guide covers the four main groups: topical NSAIDs, oral NSAIDs, paracetamol, and weak opioids. It follows NICE guidance (NG226 for osteoarthritis) and the British National Formulary recommendations used in UK clinical practice.

First-line: topical NSAID gels

For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends a topical NSAID gel as the first painkiller to try. Diclofenac (Voltarol) and ibuprofen (Nurofen) gels deliver the anti-inflammatory effect directly to the joint, with only about 5% of the drug absorbed into the bloodstream.

This means most of the benefit with much less of the risk: very low rates of stomach ulcers, kidney problems and cardiovascular events compared with oral tablets. They are well-suited for older adults and anyone with high blood pressure, kidney disease or stomach problems.

To get the most from a topical NSAID:

  • Follow the product leaflet for how much gel to apply and how often
  • Massage in as directed; wash hands after applying
  • Give topical treatment a fair trial (often around two weeks) unless your clinician advises otherwise
  • Do not apply to broken skin

Oral NSAIDs: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac

If topical NSAIDs and exercise have not controlled symptoms, your GP or rheumatology team may discuss an oral NSAID. Common UK options (see current BNF / SmPC — do not self-dose from this page) include:

  • Ibuprofen — short-acting; often used for short flares when a clinician or pharmacist confirms it is suitable.
  • Naproxen — longer-acting; sometimes preferred for ongoing arthritis pain when cardiovascular and stomach risks are acceptable.
  • Diclofenac — potent but higher cardiovascular risk in tablet form, so often used as a topical gel rather than oral tablets.

All oral NSAIDs share risks: stomach ulcers and bleeding, kidney injury, raised blood pressure, fluid retention, and a small increase in heart attack and stroke risk. Risks rise with dose, age and duration. Exact dose and duration must come from your clinician or the product label — not from educational websites.

People who need an oral NSAID for more than a few weeks are often also prescribed a proton-pump inhibitor to protect the stomach — especially if over 65, with ulcer history, or on blood-thinners. Ask your GP or pharmacist what applies to you.

Paracetamol: useful but limited

Paracetamol used to be the standard first-line painkiller for osteoarthritis. NICE downgraded it in 2022 after evidence reviews showed only modest benefit at best. It remains useful for:

  • Short-term, mild pain
  • Topping up an NSAID at flare-ups
  • People who can't take NSAIDs (kidney disease, ulcer history, certain heart conditions)

Adult labelled maximums are on the pack and in the BNF (commonly discussed as up to 4 g in 24 hours for healthy adults, with gaps between doses). Older adults, lower body weight and liver disease often need lower limits — follow the label and ask a pharmacist or GP; do not exceed labelled maximums.

Codeine, tramadol and stronger opioids

NICE no longer recommends routine opioid use for osteoarthritis. The benefits are small, and the risks — constipation, drowsiness, falls in older adults, dependence — are significant. Weak opioids (codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol) are reserved for short courses when:

  • Other treatments have genuinely been tried and failed
  • A specific event (e.g. waiting for joint replacement) requires temporary cover
  • A clear plan to stop within weeks is agreed

Strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl patches) have no routine place in arthritis care. If you have been on opioids for joint pain for more than a few months, a structured review with your GP or pain clinic is the right next step.

Who should avoid which painkiller

  • Kidney disease — avoid oral NSAIDs; topical NSAIDs and paracetamol are usually safer.
  • Heart failure or recent heart attack — avoid oral NSAIDs (especially diclofenac).
  • Stomach ulcer or bleeding history — avoid oral NSAIDs unless essential, always with a stomach-protector.
  • Asthma triggered by aspirin or NSAIDs — avoid all NSAIDs.
  • Liver disease — paracetamol dosing may need to be reduced; check with your prescriber or pharmacist before use.
  • Pregnancy — avoid NSAIDs (especially after 20 weeks); paracetamol is usually preferred.
  • Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs) — combining with NSAIDs significantly raises bleeding risk.

Combining painkillers safely

Combinations clinicians sometimes discuss (always check suitability for you):

  • Topical NSAID + paracetamol — often lower systemic risk than two oral NSAIDs
  • Oral NSAID + paracetamol — different mechanisms; stay within labelled maxima
  • Short-course weak opioid with a clear stop plan — only when a clinician recommends it

Do not combine two oral NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen and naproxen) unless a clinician explicitly directs it — risks rise without clear extra benefit. Check with a pharmacist before adding any over-the-counter painkiller to prescribed medication.

What works alongside painkillers

Painkillers are most effective when they enable the things that actually change arthritis over the long term:

  • Strengthening and aerobic exercise — the strongest evidence base for reducing arthritis pain
  • Weight management — every 1 kg lost reduces force across the knee by about 4 kg with each step
  • Heat, cold and pacing — simple, cheap and effective for daily flares
  • Steroid injections — strategic short-term relief that enables rehabilitation (see our steroids guide)
  • Disease-modifying drugs — for inflammatory arthritis, the foundation of long-term control

When to ask for a medication review

  • You've been on a daily NSAID for more than 3 months without a recent kidney and blood-pressure check
  • You're on an opioid for arthritis pain and haven't had a structured review
  • Your painkillers aren't working as well as they did
  • You're getting indigestion, black stools, or unusual bruising
  • You're stacking over-the-counter painkillers on top of prescribed ones

Key takeaways

  • Topical NSAID gels are first-line for knee and hand osteoarthritis — most of the benefit, very little of the risk.
  • Oral NSAIDs work but should be used at the lowest dose for the shortest time, almost always with a stomach-protector.
  • Paracetamol is helpful as a top-up or for people who can't take NSAIDs; it is no longer first-line.
  • Opioids have a very limited role in arthritis pain — short courses only, with a stop plan.
  • The right combination depends on your kidneys, your heart, your stomach and the rest of your medication list.
  • Painkillers buy time for the treatments that actually change arthritis: movement, strength, weight management and disease-modifying drugs.

faqs.q: What is the best painkiller for arthritis?
faqs.a: There is no single 'best' painkiller — the right choice depends on the type of arthritis, the joints involved, your other health conditions and what else you take. NICE guidance (NG226) recommends topical NSAID gels (such as diclofenac or ibuprofen) as the first-line painkiller for knee and hand osteoarthritis, with oral NSAIDs added at the lowest effective dose if topical treatment isn't enough. Paracetamol is now considered a weak option for osteoarthritis but is still useful for short-term, mild pain.

faqs.q: Are NSAIDs safe to take every day?
faqs.a: Long-term daily oral NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) raise the risk of stomach ulcers, kidney damage, raised blood pressure and cardiovascular events. They should be used at the lowest dose for the shortest time that controls symptoms, almost always with a stomach-protecting tablet (such as omeprazole or lansoprazole) if used for more than a few weeks. Topical NSAID gels are much safer for daily use because very little is absorbed into the bloodstream.

faqs.q: Can I take paracetamol and ibuprofen together for arthritis?
faqs.a: They work through different mechanisms, so clinicians sometimes advise combining them — but only within the labelled maximums on the pack / BNF and after checking interactions. Ask a pharmacist or your GP before combining painkillers, especially if you take other medicines or have kidney, stomach or heart problems.

faqs.q: What's the difference between ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac?
faqs.a: All three are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) that block the COX enzymes which drive inflammation and pain. Ibuprofen is short-acting (every 6–8 hours), naproxen is longer-acting (twice daily) and often preferred for arthritis, and diclofenac is potent but carries a higher cardiovascular risk so is usually used as a topical gel rather than tablets. The choice depends on dosing convenience and your individual risk profile.

faqs.q: Are codeine and tramadol safe for arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Weak opioids such as codeine, dihydrocodeine and tramadol can help short-term, but NICE no longer recommends routine opioid use for osteoarthritis because of limited benefit and significant risks — constipation, drowsiness, dependence and falls in older adults. They are reserved for short courses when other treatments have failed and a clear plan to stop is agreed.

faqs.q: Why does my doctor prescribe a stomach-protector with NSAIDs?
faqs.a: NSAIDs reduce the protective mucus lining of the stomach, increasing the risk of ulcers and bleeding. A proton-pump inhibitor (omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole) blocks acid production and reduces this risk significantly. Anyone aged over 65, anyone with a history of ulcers, and anyone taking NSAIDs daily for more than a few weeks should be prescribed one.

faqs.q: Can I use ibuprofen gel and ibuprofen tablets at the same time?
faqs.a: Topical NSAID absorption into the bloodstream is very low (around 5%), so combining the two is rarely a problem for short-term use. However, your prescriber may still advise against it if you are on a daily oral dose, have kidney problems, or are on other anti-inflammatory or blood-thinning medication. Check with a pharmacist.
